# Speedle — full documentation

> Speedle is an open-source (UPL-1.0) authorization engine with the SPDL policy language. It consists of ADS (decisions) and PMS (policy management), SDKs in six languages, Speedle Cloud (hosted), and Speedle AI (authorization for and with AI agents, an MCP server, and the policy-modeler skill).

This file contains the complete English documentation published at https://engine.speedle.io/, including the full reference for SPDL (Speedle Policy Definition Language). Index: https://engine.speedle.io/llms.txt. Canonical source: https://github.com/teramoby/speedle-plus (Universal Permissive License v1.0).

## About Speedle

Source: https://engine.speedle.io/about/

Speedle is an open-source (UPL-1.0) authorization engine with the SPDL policy language. It consists of ADS (decisions) and PMS (policy management), SDKs in six languages, Speedle Cloud (hosted), and Speedle AI (authorization for and with AI agents, an MCP server, and the policy-modeler skill).

Speedle was built by the team behind Oracle Entitlements Server (OES). Its design draws on many years of that team's work on earlier authorization products, including OES, BEA ALES/WLES and CrossLogix.

<p class="license origin-note"><em>This project grew out of <a href="https://github.com/oracle/speedle" style="text-decoration:underline"><svg viewBox="0 0 16 16" width="14" height="14" aria-hidden="true" focusable="false" style="fill:currentColor;vertical-align:-0.12em;margin-right:4px"><path d="M8 0C3.58 0 0 3.58 0 8c0 3.54 2.29 6.53 5.47 7.59.4.07.55-.17.55-.38 0-.19-.01-.82-.01-1.49-2.01.37-2.53-.49-2.69-.94-.09-.23-.48-.94-.82-1.13-.28-.15-.68-.52-.01-.53.63-.01 1.08.58 1.23.82.72 1.21 1.87.87 2.33.66.07-.52.28-.87.51-1.07-1.78-.2-3.64-.89-3.64-3.95 0-.87.31-1.59.82-2.15-.08-.2-.36-1.02.08-2.12 0 0 .67-.21 2.2.82.64-.18 1.32-.27 2-.27.68 0 1.36.09 2 .27 1.53-1.04 2.2-.82 2.2-.82.44 1.1.16 1.92.08 2.12.51.56.82 1.27.82 2.15 0 3.07-1.87 3.75-3.65 3.95.29.25.54.73.54 1.48 0 1.07-.01 1.93-.01 2.2 0 .21.15.46.55.38A8.013 8.013 0 0016 8c0-4.42-3.58-8-8-8z"/></svg>Oracle Speedle</a>. Its principal maintainers are the original developers of Oracle Speedle; though we have since left Oracle, we continue to maintain the project for everyone to use. The license remains the Universal Permissive License (UPL) 1.0. Questions are welcome at <a href="mailto:contact@speedle.io" style="text-decoration:underline">contact@speedle.io</a>.</em></p>

The open source version of Speedle consists of:

- SPDL (Speedle Policy Definition Language)
- Policy Management Service
- Authorization Decision Service
- Command line tool (spctl)

Speedle is licensed under Universal Permissive License v1.0. Users are free to integrate Speedle into their own systems.

## Quick Start

Source: https://engine.speedle.io/quick-start/

### Try Speedle in the Playground first

**You can try Speedle's basic features before installing anything.** Open the [Playground](https://engine.speedle.io/playground/) to edit SPDL policies, set a user, resource and action, and see real Allow/Deny decisions entirely in your browser. No Go installation or running server is required.

Continue below when you are ready to install and run Speedle locally.

### Prerequisites

Use Linux or macOS with Bash, Git, curl and **Go 1.26.10 or Go 1.27.3** (or a newer patch on the same release branch). Speedle supports patched Go 1.26 and Go 1.27 releases; this guide is verified with **Go 1.26.10 and Go 1.27.3**. Go 1.27.3 is the recommended stable release for this walkthrough.

Install Go using the [official installation instructions](https://go.dev/doc/install), then check the installed version:


```bash
go version
```

Go configures `GOROOT` and its default `GOPATH` automatically. No custom values are needed. Both routes below place the three executables in a `bin` directory.

### Install Speedle

Choose one route: route A installs the latest release, route B builds the current source. The rest of the guide uses `./bin/...` and works with either route.

#### Route A: install the latest release


```bash
GOBIN="$PWD/bin" go install github.com/teramoby/speedle-plus/cmd/...@v1.6.0
ls bin
```

`GOBIN` keeps the executables in this directory's `bin` folder; without it, Go writes them to `$(go env GOPATH)/bin`. `v1.6.0` is the latest release tag at the time of writing; `go install` builds it from the tagged source and verifies it against the Go checksum database.

#### Route B: clone and build


```bash
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/teramoby/speedle-plus.git
cd speedle-plus
mkdir -p bin
go build -o ./bin/ ./cmd/spctl ./cmd/speedle-pms ./cmd/speedle-ads
ls bin
```

The output directory contains:

```text
spctl  speedle-ads  speedle-pms
```

- `spctl`: the command line interface.
- `speedle-pms`: the Policy Management Service (PMS).
- `speedle-ads`: the Authorization Decision Service (ADS).

> **macOS:** `/usr/sbin/spctl` is Apple's Gatekeeper tool and may be selected when you run a bare `spctl` command. Call Speedle's CLI by its full path, or use `./spctl` from the directory containing it; this guide uses `./bin/spctl`. Run `command -v spctl` to check which executable your shell selects. If the release you download includes a `speedle-spctl_<os>_<arch>` asset, it is the same CLI under a name that does not collide with Apple's tool.

Modern Go uses `go build` or `go install` to build executables; `go get` manages module dependencies.

### Run Speedle

Run this walkthrough on a local development machine. `--insecure=true` enables plain HTTP for the REST examples. The gRPC servers are off unless you start them with `--grpc-endpoint`, for example `--grpc-endpoint 127.0.0.1:50001` for PMS and `--grpc-endpoint 127.0.0.1:50002` for ADS; gRPC uses the same TLS settings as REST. For production transport and authorization settings, see [Security](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/security/).

#### 1. Start the Policy Management Service

In the first terminal, from the directory that contains `bin/` (the checkout for route B):


```bash
./bin/speedle-pms --store-type file --filestore-loc ./quick-start-policies.json --endpoint 127.0.0.1:6733 --insecure=true
```

Leave it running. PMS creates `quick-start-policies.json` in this directory. Wait for the REST server to start before continuing. Both services must use this same file.

#### 2. Create policies using spctl

Open a second terminal in the same directory.

Create a service container:


```bash
./bin/spctl --pms-endpoint http://127.0.0.1:6733/policy-mgmt/v1/ create service mysvc
```

Grant `user1` permission to get or delete `res1`, and grant `role2` the same actions on `res2`:


```bash
./bin/spctl --pms-endpoint http://127.0.0.1:6733/policy-mgmt/v1/ create policy -c "grant user user1 get,del res1" --service-name=mysvc
./bin/spctl --pms-endpoint http://127.0.0.1:6733/policy-mgmt/v1/ create policy -c "grant role role2 get,del res2" --service-name=mysvc
```

Assign `role2` to `user2` on `res2`:


```bash
./bin/spctl --pms-endpoint http://127.0.0.1:6733/policy-mgmt/v1/ create rolepolicy -c "grant user user2 role2 on res2" --service-name=mysvc
```

List the service and its policies:


```bash
./bin/spctl --pms-endpoint http://127.0.0.1:6733/policy-mgmt/v1/ get service --all
```

The output includes `mysvc`, two authorization policies and one role policy.

#### 3. Start the Authorization Decision Service

Open a third terminal in the same directory:


```bash
./bin/speedle-ads --store-type file --filestore-loc ./quick-start-policies.json --endpoint 127.0.0.1:6734 --insecure=true
```

Leave it running and wait for its REST server to start.

#### 4. Verify authorization decisions

Run these requests in the second terminal. The first request checks the direct grant to `user1`:


```bash
curl --fail --silent --show-error --header 'Content-Type: application/json' --data '{"subject":{"principals":[{"type":"user","name":"user1"}]},"serviceName":"mysvc","resource":"res1","action":"get"}' http://127.0.0.1:6734/authz-check/v1/is-allowed
```

The response contains `"allowed":true`.

The next request checks the role grant to `user2`:


```bash
curl --fail --silent --show-error --header 'Content-Type: application/json' --data '{"subject":{"principals":[{"type":"user","name":"user2"}]},"serviceName":"mysvc","resource":"res2","action":"get"}' http://127.0.0.1:6734/authz-check/v1/is-allowed
```

The response contains `"allowed":true`.

A user without a matching grant is denied:


```bash
curl --fail --silent --show-error --header 'Content-Type: application/json' --data '{"subject":{"principals":[{"type":"user","name":"user3"}]},"serviceName":"mysvc","resource":"res1","action":"get"}' http://127.0.0.1:6734/authz-check/v1/is-allowed
```

The response contains `"allowed":false`.

The `reason` field explains each decision. `0` (`GRANT_POLICY_FOUND`) means a grant policy matched; `3` (`NO_APPLICABLE_POLICIES`) means no policy applied, so Speedle denies by default. The [Authorization Decisions](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/decisions/) page lists every reason code.

#### 5. Add a conditional (ABAC) policy

Create a grant that applies only when the request carries a `clearance` attribute of at least 3:


```bash
./bin/spctl --pms-endpoint http://127.0.0.1:6733/policy-mgmt/v1/ create policy -c "grant user user1 get res3 if clearance >= 3" --service-name=mysvc
```

The policy enforcement point (PEP) supplies request attributes, and a condition is evaluated only against the attributes in the request. The `clearance` values below demonstrate the request format only: a real PEP must obtain attribute values from trusted sources, such as authenticated token claims or a trusted store, and never from the request being authorized. A request that omits `clearance` does not match this grant.

With `clearance` set to 4, the request is allowed:


```bash
curl --fail --silent --show-error --header 'Content-Type: application/json' --data '{"subject":{"principals":[{"type":"user","name":"user1"}]},"serviceName":"mysvc","resource":"res3","action":"get","attributes":[{"name":"clearance","type":"numeric","value":4}]}' http://127.0.0.1:6734/authz-check/v1/is-allowed
```

The response contains `"allowed":true` and `"reason":0`.

With `clearance` set to 2, the condition does not match, so no policy applies and the request is denied:


```bash
curl --fail --silent --show-error --header 'Content-Type: application/json' --data '{"subject":{"principals":[{"type":"user","name":"user1"}]},"serviceName":"mysvc","resource":"res3","action":"get","attributes":[{"name":"clearance","type":"numeric","value":2}]}' http://127.0.0.1:6734/authz-check/v1/is-allowed
```

The response contains `"allowed":false` and `"reason":3`.

When finished, press **Ctrl+C** in the PMS and ADS terminals. The policy file remains in this directory; use a fresh file for another run of the creation commands.

For TLS configuration, see [Message security](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/security/#protect-both-api-transports). For other deployment types, see [Deployment](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/deployment/).

## Overview

Source: https://engine.speedle.io/docs/overview/

Speedle is an open-source authorization engine. Applications send it a question such as "may this user perform this action on this resource?", and Speedle answers allow or deny according to centrally managed policies. This page connects common authorization terms to the Speedle components that implement them, and links to the guides that cover each one.

The examples below use a service named `library`. Each policy was created through the Policy Management Service REST API and each decision was returned by the Authorization Decision Service REST API. The reason codes are listed in [Authorization Decisions](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/decisions/).

### Authorization engine

An authorization engine evaluates access requests against policies and returns a decision, so that the authorization logic lives outside application code. Speedle consists of a [Policy Management Service (PMS), a policy repository and an Authorization Decision Service (ADS)](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/architecture/). The ADS can run as a standalone service or be [embedded in a Go application](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/deployment-embeded/).

### Authorization and access control

Authentication establishes who a caller is; authorization decides what that caller may do. Access control is the enforcement of those decisions. Speedle handles authorization only: it receives an already-authenticated subject and returns a decision, which the calling application or gateway enforces. See [Authorization Decisions](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/decisions/).

### Fine-grained access control (FGA)

Fine-grained access control decides access per user, per resource and per action, optionally taking request context into account, rather than granting broad access to a whole application. A Speedle policy names the principals, the actions and the resource, and may add a condition. A role policy can assign a role for one resource only. See [SPDL](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/spdl/).

### PAP: Policy Administration Point

The PAP is where policies are created and managed. In Speedle this is the PMS, used through its [REST API](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/api/management_api/), gRPC API or the `spctl` command-line tool. See [Policy Management](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/pms/policy-mgmt/).

### PDP: Policy Decision Point

The PDP evaluates a request against policies and returns a decision. In Speedle this is the ADS, or the embedded evaluator when Speedle runs inside a Go process. A decision request looks like this:

```bash
curl --header 'Content-Type: application/json' --data '{"subject":{"principals":[{"type":"user","name":"alice"}]},"serviceName":"library","resource":"book","action":"update"}' http://127.0.0.1:6734/authz-check/v1/is-allowed
```

With the RBAC policies below, the response is `{"allowed":true,"reason":0}`. See the [decision API](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/api/decision_api/).

### PEP: Policy Enforcement Point

The PEP intercepts an access attempt, asks the PDP for a decision and enforces it. Speedle does not ship a general-purpose PEP; the PEP is the application or gateway that calls the ADS through its REST or gRPC API, or that embeds the evaluator in Go. See [Integrations](https://engine.speedle.io/integrations/) for the supported interfaces.

### PIP: Policy Information Point

The PIP supplies extra information needed to evaluate a policy. In Speedle, this information comes from request attributes and [built-in attributes](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/spdl/#2-2-1-built-in-attributes), from the [token asserter](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/assertor/), which turns an identity token into a subject, and from [custom functions](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/custom-function/), which call external REST endpoints during evaluation.

### XACML

XACML (eXtensible Access Control Markup Language) is an OASIS standard that defines both a policy language and the PAP/PDP/PEP/PIP architecture. Speedle follows the same division of roles, but its policy language is SPDL, not XACML, and it cannot import XACML policies.

### RBAC: role-based access control

In RBAC, permissions are granted to roles and roles are assigned to users or groups. Speedle uses a policy to grant permissions to a role, and a role policy to assign the role:

```text
grant role librarian read,update book
grant user alice librarian
```

`alice` may update `book` (reason 0, grant policy found); `bob`, who has no role, is denied (reason 3, no applicable policies). Roles can also be assigned only for a particular resource; see [Policy Management](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/pms/policy-mgmt/) and [Global Policy](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/pms/global-policy/).

### ABAC: attribute-based access control

In ABAC, the decision depends on attributes of the subject, resource, action or environment. In Speedle, any policy or role policy can carry an `if` condition over attributes:

```text
grant user bob read report if department == 'finance'
```

A request from `bob` with the string attribute `department` set to `finance` is allowed (reason 0); with `sales`, or without the attribute, it is denied (reason 3). See [Condition](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/spdl/#condition).

### PBAC: policy-based access control

PBAC manages access through centrally defined policies instead of permissions embedded in each application. All Speedle policies are kept in the PMS and evaluated with two fixed rules: deny overrides grant, and a request with no applicable grant is denied.

```text
grant group staff read,delete journal
deny user carol delete journal
```

`carol`, a member of `staff`, is denied `delete` on `journal` (reason 1, deny policy found); `erin`, also in `staff`, is allowed (reason 0).

### Identity and IAM

Identity and access management (IAM) covers both proving who a user is and deciding what the user may do. Speedle is not an identity provider and does not authenticate users. It consumes identities: principals can be qualified by an [identity domain](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/idd/), and identity tokens can be resolved by the [token asserter](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/assertor/).

```text
grant user dave from github read code
```

`dave` from the `github` identity domain may read `code` (reason 0); `dave` from `corp`, or with no identity domain, is denied (reason 3).

### Zero trust

Zero trust grants no access on the basis of network location and checks every request. Speedle supports this as the decision service: the ADS evaluates each request it receives, and anything not explicitly granted is denied. Authentication, device trust and network controls are outside Speedle's scope.

### SPDL: Speedle Policy Definition Language

SPDL stands for Speedle Policy Definition Language. It is the language used to write Speedle policies and role policies, for example `grant role librarian read,update book`. See the [SPDL reference](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/spdl/).

### Integrations

Other applications call the ADS through its [REST or gRPC APIs](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/api/), or embed the evaluator in Go; see [Deployment](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/deployment/). The [Integrations](https://engine.speedle.io/integrations/) page lists the APIs, SDKs, embedded mode and policy stores that ship today.

## Architecture

Source: https://engine.speedle.io/docs/architecture/

### Modules

Speedle is an authorization engine comprised of these components:

- Policy Management Service (PMS) API - Manages the authorization and role policies, and the objects from which they are created.

- Policy repository - Stores all the policy artifacts. The policy repository can be a json file, or a persistent store such as a database or etcd.

- Authorization Decision Service (ADS) API - Evaluates the authorization requests against the applicable policies and returns GRANT/DENY decisions.

This diagram shows the interaction between these components.

<img src="https://engine.speedle.io/img/speedle/spdlarch.jpg" width="524" height="241" loading="lazy" />

(1) Users create/manage policies through the Policy Management Service API.  
(2) The Policy Management Service persists the policies in the policy repository.  
(3) The policies are provisioned from the policy repository to the Authorization Decision Service API.  
(4) Users systems invoke the Authorization Decision Service API for authorization checks.

If you are familiar with the XACML model, the Policy Management Service (PMS) serves as the Policy Administration Point (PAP), and the Authorization Decision Service (ADS) serves as the Policy Decision Point (PDP).

## SPDL - Speedle Policy Definition Language

Source: https://engine.speedle.io/docs/spdl/

SPDL is the language for writing Speedle policies and role policies. This page covers the syntax, naming rules and examples.


<aside class="docs-callout" aria-labelledby="spdl-callout-title">
  <p class="docs-callout-eyebrow">Speedle policy modeler · Open source skill</p>
  <p class="docs-callout-title" id="spdl-callout-title">Write SPDL with AI</p>
  <p>The open-source Speedle policy modeler skill turns your requirements and policy documents into an SPDL model with allow and deny test cases, validated with <code>spctl check</code>.</p>
  <p class="docs-callout-actions"><a class="button primary" href="https://ai.speedle.io/#policy-modeler">Try the policy modeler skill</a> <a class="button secondary" href="https://github.com/teramoby/ai.speedle.io/tree/main/skills/speedle-policy-modeler">Source on GitHub</a></p>
</aside>

### Syntax

<picture><source srcset="https://engine.speedle.io/img/speedle/spdl-syntax.webp" type="image/webp"><img src="https://engine.speedle.io/img/speedle/spdl-syntax.png" alt="Basic policy definition syntax" width="2222" height="971" fetchpriority="high"></picture>

#### Keywords

`grant`, `deny`, `user`, `group`, `entity`, `role`, `from`, `on`, `if` and `in` have special meanings in their syntax positions. Statement keywords are case-insensitive. In conditions, use `in` or `IN`; function names are case-sensitive. Principal, action and resource names are also case-sensitive. The current parser accepts keyword-like names in some name positions, so a blanket prohibition is not a validation rule. Prefer unambiguous names for review and client interoperability.

#### Naming Convention

Prefer simple, stable identifiers. Quote names containing whitespace or separators using the parser’s single- or double-quoted form, and test the actual input. Historical Java regular-expression character classes are not a validation contract for the Go parser. The `expr:` resource prefix uses Go regular expressions, not shell globs. Attribute and function names in conditions are described below.

#### Syntax

<pre>
POLICY = EFFECT SUBJECT ACTION RESOURCE [if CONDITION]
EFFECT = grant | deny
SUBJECT = AND_PRINCIPALS (, AND_PRINCIPALS)*
AND_PRINCIPALS = PRINCIPAL | \( PRINCIPAL_LIST \)
PRINCIPAL_LIST = PRINCIPAL (, PRINCIPAL)*
PRINCIPAL = PRINCIPAL_TYPE PRINCIPAL_NAME [PRINCIPAL_IDD]
PRINCIPAL_TYPE = user|group|entity|role
PRINCIPAL_IDD = from IDD_IDENTIFIER
IDD_IDENTIFIER = NAME
ACTION = (ACTION_IDENTIFIER)(, ACTION_IDENTIFIER)*
RESOURCE = RESOURCE_IDENTIFIER
PRINCIPAL_NAME = NAME
ACTION_IDENTIFIER = NAME
RESOURCE_IDENTIFIER = NAME
</pre>
<pre>
ROLE_POLICY = EFFECT SUBJECT ROLE (on RESOURCE)? [if CONDITION]
EFFECT = grant | deny
SUBJECT = PRINCIPAL (, PRINCIPAL)*
PRINCIPAL = PRINCIPAL_TYPE PRINCIPAL_NAME [PRINCIPAL_IDD]
PRINCIPAL_TYPE = user|group|entity|role
PRINCIPAL_IDD = from IDD_IDENTIFIER
IDD_IDENTIFIER = NAME
ROLE = (role)? SUBJECT_IDENTIFIER
RESOURCE = RESOURCE_IDENTIFIER
SUBJECT_IDENTIFIER = NAME
RESOURCE_IDENTIFIER = NAME
</pre>

### Examples

Role inheritance: the subject of a role policy can be another role, so `manager` also holds every role assigned to `employee`.

```text
grant role manager employee
```

Deny over grant: an applicable deny wins over a grant. Here `carol` is in `staff` and is still denied `delete` on `journal`.

```text
grant group staff read,delete journal
deny user carol delete journal
```

A condition: the policy applies only when the condition is true.

```text
grant user bob read report if department == 'finance'
```

These are SPDL statements, not a complete service fixture; see [Policy Management](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/pms/policy-mgmt/) for services, resource-scoped roles and complete decision examples.

### Condition

#### 1. Overview

Condition is supported in both policy and role policy definitions. The policy or role policy can take effect _only_ when the condition is met.

The policy enforcement point (PEP) must supply every custom attribute your policies reference; built-in attributes such as `request_user` and `request_time` are provided by ADS. Attributes supplied by the PEP come from the caller's trusted application or service, not from end users, and the PEP is responsible for the values it sends. Attributes supplied by the PEP take precedence over built-in attributes with the same name; in particular, never forward untrusted end-user input as `request_user`, `request_time` or any other built-in attribute name.

A condition that references an attribute missing from the request does not match. A conditional `deny` therefore does not apply when its attribute is absent. Make sure the PEP always supplies the attributes your deny conditions use, and test those requests.

This document focuses on what a condition is, and how to write a condition.

#### 2. Condition

A condition is a bool expression that is constructed using attributes, functions, constants, operators, comparators or parenthesis and produces a bool value.

##### 2.1 Data Types

The data type of an attribute value and constant can be a string, numeric, bool, datetime or an array of string, numeric, bool, datetime.  
The data types and the corresponding supported operators and comparators are listed in following table.

 <table class="bordered striped">
    <thead>
      <tr>
        <th>Data Type</th>
        <th>Operators</th>
        <th>Comparators</th>
        <th>Comment</th>
      </tr>
    </thead>
    <tbody>
      <tr>
        <td>string</td>
        <td>+</td>
        <td>== <br> != <br> =~ <br> > <br> >= <br> < <br> <= <br>
        </td>
        <td>'+' is for string concatenation <br> '=~' is for regular expr matching, see the annotation below the table.</td>
      </tr>
      <tr>
        <td>numeric</td>
        <td> + <br> - <br> * <br> / <br> %</td>
        <td>== <br> != <br>  > <br> >= <br> < <br> <= </td>
        <td></td>
      </tr>
      <tr>
        <td>bool</td>
        <td>&& <br> || <br> !</td>
        <td>== <br>!=</td>
        <td></td>
      </tr>
      <tr>
        <td>datetime</td>
        <td></td>
        <td>== <br> != <br> > <br> >= <br> < <br> <=</td>
        <td></td>
      </tr>
      <tr>
        <td>array</td>
        <td></td>
        <td>in</td>
        <td>membership 'in' operator: left side should be a single type(string, numeric, bool, datetime), right side should be an array</td>
      </tr>
    </tbody>
    <tfoot>
    </tfoot>
  </table>

Most comparators are self explanatory, here is the annotation for `"=~"`:  
`"=~"` is the regex comparator. It uses Go's standard regexp flavor of regex. The left side is expected to be the candidate string; the right side is the pattern.
`"=~"` returns whether or not the candidate string matches the regex pattern given on the right.

- Left side: string
- Right side: string
- Returns: bool

##### 2.2 Attributes

An attribute in a condition represents a variable. The attribute value is determined at runtime, obtained from either the Authorization Decision Service (ADS) runtime or the PEP.
Built-in attributes are those values that are populated by the ADS runtime.
Customer attributes are those values that are provided by the PEP — the caller's trusted application or service — when asking ADS for authorization decisions, not by end users. The PEP is responsible for the values it sends. Attributes supplied by the PEP take precedence over built-in attributes with the same name, so a PEP must not forward untrusted end-user input under a built-in attribute name.

###### 2.2.1 Built-in Attributes

Built-in attributes are as follows:

<table class="bordered striped">
    <thead>
      <tr>
        <th>Built-in Attribute Name</th>
        <th>Data Type </th>
        <th>Sample Value</th>
        <th>Definition</th>
      </tr>
    </thead>
    <tbody>
      <tr>
        <td>request_user</td>
        <td>string</td>
        <td>"Alice"</td>
        <td>The user information in the subject who is requesting to act on a resource</td>
      </tr>
      <tr>
        <td>request_groups</td>
        <td>[]string</td>
        <td>[]string{"managers"}</td>
        <td>The groups information in the subject who is requesting to act on a resource</td>
      </tr>
      <tr>
        <td>request_entity</td>
        <td>string</td>
        <td>"/org1/service1"</td>
        <td>The service name or other entity info in the subject which the service or program is requesting to act on a resource</td>
      </tr>
      <tr>
        <td>request_resource</td>
        <td>string</td>
        <td>"commercialLoans"</td>
        <td>The resource on which the subject is to act</td>
      </tr>
      <tr>
        <td>request_action</td>
        <td>string</td>
        <td>"issue" </td>
        <td>The action that the subject is to carry out on a resource </td>
      </tr>
      <tr>
        <td>request_time</td>
        <td>datetime</td>
        <td>'2019-01-02T15:04:05-07:00'</td>
        <td>The date and time when the request happens</td>
      </tr>
      <tr>
        <td>request_year</td>
        <td>int</td>
        <td>2019</td>
        <td>The year when the request happens</td>
      </tr>
      <tr>
        <td>request_month</td>
        <td>int</td>
        <td>1, 2, ... 12</td>
        <td>The month when the request happens</td>
      </tr>
      <tr>
        <td>request_day</td>
        <td>int</td>
        <td>1, 2, ... 31</td>
        <td>The day in a month when the request happens</td>
      </tr>
      <tr>
        <td>request_hour</td>
        <td>int</td>
        <td>0, 1, ... 23</td>
        <td>The hour in a day when the request happens</td>
      </tr>
      <tr>
        <td>request_weekday</td>
        <td>string</td>
        <td>"Sunday", "Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday"</td>
        <td>The day of the week when the request happens</td>
      </tr>
    </tbody>
    <tfoot>
    </tfoot>
  </table>

###### 2.2.2 Customer Attributes

###### 2.2.2.1 name

For portable condition references, prefer `[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9_]*` and avoid built-in attribute/function names. The REST layer actually accepts up to 256 ASCII letters, digits, underscores, hyphens and dots. Test expression references containing a hyphen or dot rather than assuming they are ordinary identifiers instead of operators.

###### 2.2.2.2 value

When customer attributes are used in a condition, the customer needs to pass the customer attribute values when requesting an isAllowed result. If the request does not carry an attribute that a condition references, the condition does not match; a conditional `deny` does not apply in that case. Ensure the PEP supplies every attribute your deny conditions use, and test those requests.

- Passing attribute values in Golang API  
   Adhere to these rules when passing customer attribute values to a Golang API:

  - Use Golang bool type for bool attribute value.
  - Use Golang string type for string attribute value.
  - Use Golang float64 type for any numeric attribute value.
  - For datetime attribute value, use a Golang float64 representation of that datetime's Unix time (using `time.Time.Unix()`).
  - Use Golang []interface{} for array attribute value.

- Passing attribute values in REST API  
   Adhere to these rules when passing customer attribute values to a REST API:
  - Attribute is a struct, which contains name, type, value of the attribute. See the REST API for details.
  - Attribute type can be only "string", "numeric", "bool" or "datetime".
  - Attribute value can be a single value or a slice.

##### 2.3 Constants

Supported data types:

- string: single quotes, 'foobar'
- numeric: 10, 3.1415926
- bool: true or false
- datetime: single quotes, conform to RFC3339. Datetime of RFC3339 format is YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm:SS[.sssssssss]Z, Z is [+|-]HH:mm.
- array: array of type string, numeric, bool, datetime

The following table shows sample constants.

<table class="bordered striped">
    <thead>
      <tr>
        <th>Data Type</th>
        <th>Constant Samples </th>
        <th>Array Constant Samples</th>
      </tr>
    </thead>
    <tbody>
      <tr>
        <td>string</td>
        <td>'a string'</td>
        <td>('string1', 'string2')</td>
      </tr>
      <tr>
        <td>bool</td>
        <td>true <br> false</td>
        <td>(true, false, true)</td>
      </tr>
      <tr>
        <td>numeric / float</td>
        <td>2.1</td>
        <td>(1, 2, 3.1)</td>
      </tr>
      <tr>
        <td>datetime</td>
        <td>'2006-01-02T15:04:05-07:00'</td>
        <td>('2016-01-02T15:04:05-07:00', '2019-01-02T15:04:05-07:00')</td>
      </tr>
    </tbody>
    <tfoot>
    </tfoot>
  </table>

##### 2.4 Functions

Use functions when existing operators or comparators do not meet customer requirements.

###### 2.4.1 Built-in Functions

Speedle provides the following built-in functions.

<table class="bordered striped">
    <thead>
      <tr>
        <th>Built-in Function Name</th>
        <th>Functionality </th>
        <th>Input and Data Type </th>
        <th>Output and Data Type</th>
        <th>Sample Usage</th>
      </tr>
    </thead>
    <tbody>
       <tr>
        <td>Sqrt</td>
        <td>Square root of a numeric</td>
        <td>One numeric parameter</td>
        <td>numeric</td>
        <td>Sqrt(x)<br>Sqrt(64)</td>
      </tr>
       <tr>
        <td>Max</td>
        <td>Get the max numeric in a set</td>
        <td>1+ numeric parameters</td>
        <td>numeric</td>
        <td>Max(1, 4, x)</td>
      </tr>
       <tr>
        <td>Min</td>
        <td>Get the min numeric in a set</td>
        <td>1+ numeric parameters</td>
        <td>numeric</td>
        <td>Min(x, 5, z)</td>
      </tr>
       <tr>
        <td>Sum</td>
        <td>Get the sum of a set of numeric</td>
        <td>1+ numeric parameters</td>
        <td>numeric</td>
        <td>Sum(1, 3, 5, 7, x)</td>
      </tr>
      <tr>
        <td>Avg</td>
        <td>Get the average value for a set of numeric</td>
        <td>1+ numeric parameters</td>
        <td>numeric</td>
        <td>Avg(x, 8, 10)</td>
      </tr>
      <tr>
        <td>IsSubSet</td>
        <td>Check if the first set/array is a subset of the second set/array</td>
        <td>2 sets/arrays, elements of the 2 sets/arrays have same data type</td>
        <td>bool</td>
        <td>IsSubSet(s1, s2)</td>
      </tr>
    </tbody>
    <tfoot>
    </tfoot>
  </table>

Numeric built-ins reject non-finite inputs/results and negative square roots with `BuiltInFuncError`. A failed function makes its condition nonmatching, as with other runtime condition errors. `Sum()` and `Avg()` retain their historical empty-input result of zero. `IsSubSet` ignores duplicate elements, rejects unsupported or mixed element types, and retains the historical false result for an empty set. SPDL quoted names preserve literal backslashes; use the other quote style when a name contains a quote. Statements must be fully consumed: trailing text, incomplete conditions and unclosed name quotes are rejected.

###### 2.4.2 Custom Functions

Customers can also expose their own functions through a REST API, and use custom functions in a condition expression.  
For details, see [custom function](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/custom-function/).

##### 2.5 Operator/Comparator Precedence

###### 2.5.1 Precedence order

When two operators share an operand, the operator with the higher precedence goes first. For example, `1 + 2 * 3` is treated as `1 + (2 * 3)`, whereas `1 * 2 + 3` is treated as `(1 * 2) + 3` because multiplication has a higher precedence than addition.

###### 2.5.2 Associativity

When an expression has two operators with the same precedence, the expression is evaluated according to its associativity. `72 / 2 / 3`is treated as `(72 / 2) / 3` because the `/` operator has left-to-right associativity. Some operators are not associative: for example, the expressions `(x <= y <= z)` and `x++--` are invalid.

###### 2.5.3 Precedence and Associativity of Supported Operators and Comparators

The following table summarizes the documented expression syntax from highest to lowest precedence. Comparisons bind before logical AND/OR; use parentheses to make complex conditions clear.

<table class="bordered striped"><thead><tr><th>Precedence (highest first)</th><th>Operator/comparator</th><th>Associativity</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>1</td><td>( )</td><td>N/A</td></tr><tr><td>2</td><td>function call</td><td>N/A</td></tr><tr><td>3</td><td>! and unary -</td><td>Right to left</td></tr><tr><td>4</td><td>* / %</td><td>Left to right</td></tr><tr><td>5</td><td>+ -</td><td>Left to right</td></tr><tr><td>6</td><td>== != =~ &gt; &gt;= &lt; &lt;= in</td><td>N/A</td></tr><tr><td>7</td><td>&amp;&amp;</td><td>Left to right</td></tr><tr><td>8</td><td>||</td><td>Left to right</td></tr></tbody></table>

##### 2.6 Sample Conditions

<table class="bordered striped">
    <thead>
      <tr>
        <th>Condition</th>
        <th>Comment</th>
      </tr>
    </thead>
    <tbody>
    <tr><td>a=='abc'</td><td> Value of attribute 'a' equals 'abc'</td></tr>
    <tr><td>a!='abc'</td><td></td></tr>
    <tr><td>a>='abc'</td><td></td></tr>
    <tr><td>a+b=='ab'</td><td></td></tr>
    <tr><td>a=~'^get.*'</td><td>Value of attribute 'a' matches regular expression '^get.*'</td></tr>
<tr><td>a==123</td><td></td></tr>
<tr><td>a-b>123</td><td></td></tr>
<tr><td>a in (1, 2, 3) </td><td>Value of attribute 'a' is one of 1, 2, 3 </td></tr>
<tr><td>'manager' in a </td><td>'a' is an attribute of string array, 'manager' is one of the array element </td></tr>
<tr><td>IsSubSet(e, ('s1', 's2', 's3'))</td><td>'e' is an attribute of string array/set, and e is subset of array/set ('s1', 's2', 's3')</td></tr>
<tr><td>a in (1, 2, 3) && (b==c &#124;&#124; d==3) && IsSubSet(e, ('s1', 's2', 's3'))</td><td></td></tr>
<tr><td>request_year==2019 && request_month==12 </td><td> request_year and request_month are built-in attributes. The year when a resource is accessed equals 2019, and the month when the resource is accessed is 12</td></tr>
 </tbody>
    <tfoot>
    </tfoot>
  </table>

#### Condition Definition

Condition should be a valid bool expression. The following summarizes common expressions; validate exact inputs against the current parser:

```
BoolExpr: ('!')BoolExpr
          | BoolExpr ('&&'|'||') BoolExpr
		  | BoolConstant
		  | Attribute
		  | Function
		  | RelationalExpr
		  | '(' BoolExpr ')'


RelationalExpr: NumericExpr ('=='|'!='|'>'|'>='|'<'|'<=') NumericExpr
              | StringExpr ('=='|'!='|'=~'|'>'|'>='|'<'|'<=') StringExpr
			  | BoolExpr ('=='|'!=') BoolExpr
			  | DateTimeExpr ('=='|'!='|'>'|'>='|'<'|'<=') DateTimeExpr
			  | (NumericExpr|StringExpr|BoolExpr|DateTimeExpr) ('in') ArrayExpr


NumericExpr: NumericExpr('+'|'-'|'*'|'/'|'%')NumericExpr
           | NumericConstant
		   | Attribute
		   | Function
		   | '(' NumericExpr ')'

StringExpr: StringExpr('+') StringExpr
           | StringConstant
		   | Attribute
		   | Function
           | '(' StringExpr ')'

DateTimeExpr: DateTimeConstant
           | Attribute
           | Function

ArrayExpr: ArrayConstant
         | Attribute
         | Function

ArrayConstant: '('Constant [, Constant]* ')'

Constant: NumericConstant
         |StringConstant
         |BoolConstant
         |DateTimeConstant

NumericConstant: any numeric float64 data
StringConstant: single quoted string, for example, 'string1'
BoolConstant: true|false
DateTimeConstant: single quoted datetime, datetime should conform to the format defined by RFC3339: YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm:SS[.sssssssss]Z, Z is [+|-]HH:mm. For example, '2016-01-02T15:04:05-07:00'

Attribute: attribute name should conform to  [a-zA-Z]+[a-zA-Z0-9_]*, prefer simple portable identifiers; REST attribute names are limited to 256 ASCII characters
Function: FunctionName '(' Argument [,Argument]* ')'

```

## Authorization Decisions

Source: https://engine.speedle.io/docs/decisions/

### What is an authorization decision?

Speedle evaluates a subject, action and resource within a service. The application must enforce the result. Treat an evaluation error or timeout separately from a normal Deny and fail closed. REST, gRPC and embedded Go APIs have different wire representations; use their respective [contracts](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/api/).

### Before running the examples

Build `./bin/spctl`, `./bin/speedle-pms` and `./bin/speedle-ads` using the [quick start](https://engine.speedle.io/quick-start/). Use Go 1.26.10 or Go 1.27.3 (or a newer patch on the same release branch), Bash, curl and Python 3. Run each terminal from the repository root. Use a fresh policy file for this page; reset it only after stopping both services.

Initialize an empty policy file:


```bash
printf '{}\n' > docs-policies.json
```

In terminal one, start PMS and leave it running:


```bash
./bin/speedle-pms --store-type file --filestore-loc ./docs-policies.json --endpoint 127.0.0.1:6733 --grpc-endpoint 127.0.0.1:0 --insecure=true
```

In terminal two, start ADS and leave it running:


```bash
./bin/speedle-ads --store-type file --filestore-loc ./docs-policies.json --endpoint 127.0.0.1:6734 --grpc-endpoint 127.0.0.1:0 --insecure=true
```

Run the remaining commands in a third terminal. PMS and ADS share the file; watch propagates changes asynchronously. Confirm the intended update has reached ADS before relying on it. `--insecure=true` is only for this loopback example; see [security](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/security/) for production connections. Explicit PMS addresses avoid changing `~/.spctlconfig`. Stop both server terminals with Ctrl-C when finished.


### Create a reproducible policy set

The [fixture](https://github.com/teramoby/speedle-plus/blob/master/website/tests/examples/bookstore.json) assigns Alan `role1` and `role2`; `role1` may download `/books/HarryPotter`.


```bash
./bin/spctl --pms-endpoint http://127.0.0.1:6733/policy-mgmt/v1/ create service --json-file website/tests/examples/bookstore.json
```


### Get a decision

Alan is allowed; Bob is denied because no grant applies.


```bash
curl --fail --silent --show-error -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"subject":{"principals":[{"type":"user","name":"Alan"}]},"serviceName":"onlineBookStore","resource":"/books/HarryPotter","action":"download"}' \
  http://127.0.0.1:6734/authz-check/v1/is-allowed
```



```bash
curl --fail --silent --show-error -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"subject":{"principals":[{"type":"user","name":"Bob"}]},"serviceName":"onlineBookStore","resource":"/books/HarryPotter","action":"download"}' \
  http://127.0.0.1:6734/authz-check/v1/is-allowed
```


Successful decisions return `{"allowed":true,"reason":0}` or a corresponding Deny object. HTTP errors return an error response, not a successful grant. Reason codes are:

| Code | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | GRANT_POLICY_FOUND |
| 1 | DENY_POLICY_FOUND |
| 2 | SERVICE_NOT_FOUND |
| 3 | NO_APPLICABLE_POLICIES |
| 4 | ERROR_IN_EVALUATION |
| 5 | DISCOVER_MODE |
| 6 | REASON_NOT_AVAILABLE |

`DISCOVER_MODE` is not a production authorization grant. `REASON_NOT_AVAILABLE` is the fallback reason value. Do not assume these numbers are HTTP status codes.

### Get granted roles


```bash
curl --fail --silent --show-error -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"subject":{"principals":[{"type":"user","name":"Alan"}]},"serviceName":"onlineBookStore","resource":"/books/HarryPotter","action":"download"}' \
  http://127.0.0.1:6734/authz-check/v1/all-granted-roles
```


Expected roles are `role1` and `role2` (ordering is not significant). Include `resource` when querying resource-scoped role assignments.

### Get granted permissions


```bash
curl --fail --silent --show-error -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"subject":{"principals":[{"type":"user","name":"Alan"}]},"serviceName":"onlineBookStore","resource":"/books/HarryPotter","action":"download"}' \
  http://127.0.0.1:6734/authz-check/v1/all-granted-permissions
```


Expected permission: resource `/books/HarryPotter`, action `download`. This API describes effective granted permissions; enforce a particular operation with `is-allowed` rather than treating a permission-list response as a replacement for request evaluation.

### Attributes, diagnosis and token identity

REST request attributes are typed objects in an array. For example, an attribute item is:

```json
{
  "name": "clearance",
  "type": "numeric",
  "value": 4
}
```

Embedded Go attributes are `map[string]interface{}`; diagnostic response attributes are also an object, not that request array. See [SPDL](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/spdl/) for types and conditions, [diagnosis](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/pms/diagnosis/) for evaluation detail, and [token assertion](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/assertor/) for configured token validation.

The policy enforcement point (PEP) must supply every custom attribute your policies reference (built-in attributes such as `request_user` and `request_time` are provided by ADS). The PEP is the caller's trusted application or service, not the end user, and it is responsible for the attribute values it sends; never forward untrusted end-user input under a built-in attribute name. A condition on an attribute missing from the request does not match, so a conditional deny does not apply when its attribute is absent. Ensure the PEP supplies every attribute your deny conditions use, and test those requests.

## Speedle Policy

Source: https://engine.speedle.io/docs/pms/

-   [Policy Management](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/pms/policy-mgmt/)
-   [Global Policy](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/pms/global-policy/)
-   [Policy Discovery](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/pms/discover/)
-   [Policy Diagnosis](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/pms/diagnosis/)

## Policy Management

Source: https://engine.speedle.io/docs/pms/policy-mgmt/

### What is a Speedle policy?

The Policy Management Service (PMS) manages services, authorization policies, role policies and custom functions. A policy store persists those objects using a registered [storage backend](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/store/).

<img src="https://engine.speedle.io/img/speedle/policystore.png" width="1942" height="540" loading="lazy"/>

### Services and authorization policies

A service scopes its policies. An authorization policy grants or denies a principal permission to perform an action on a resource, optionally subject to a condition. Except for [global role policies](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/pms/global-policy/), policies do not automatically apply in another service.

<img src="https://engine.speedle.io/img/speedle/authzpolicy.png" width="1770" height="444" loading="lazy"/>

```text
grant group Administrators list,watch,get expr:^c1/default/core/pods/.*$
```

This regular expression matches resources under `c1/default/core/pods/`. It does not match `c1/default/core/podssecret` or an extra prefix before `c1`. `expr:` uses regular-expression matching, not shell globs: use `.*` for arbitrary characters and `^`/`$` when the complete identifier must match.

### Role policies

<img src="https://engine.speedle.io/img/speedle/rolepolicy.png" width="1598" height="436" loading="lazy"/>

```text
grant user alan manager on res1
grant role manager update res1
```

The first statement assigns Alan a resource-scoped role; the second grants that role an operation. Assigning a role alone does not create permissions. An applicable explicit deny overrides a grant.

### Principals and conditions

A principal may be a user, group, entity or role. An entity represents a non-human identity, such as a service. Integrations must derive these identities from trusted sources.

<img src="https://engine.speedle.io/img/speedle/principal.png" width="1769" height="505" loading="lazy"/>

An AND group requires every listed principal; separate groups are alternatives. For example, both roles below must apply:

<img src="https://engine.speedle.io/img/speedle/andprincipal.png" width="1584" height="349" loading="lazy"/>

```text
grant (role designer, role dba) update db_design_doc
```

A resource names the protected object; an action names an application operation. A condition is a Boolean expression evaluated from trusted attributes, constants, operators and supported functions.

<img src="https://engine.speedle.io/img/speedle/resource.png" width="1732" height="349" loading="lazy"/>

See [SPDL](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/spdl/) for grammar and [RBAC](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/overview/)/[ABAC](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/overview/) for complete decision examples.

### Before running the examples

Build `./bin/spctl`, `./bin/speedle-pms` and `./bin/speedle-ads` using the [quick start](https://engine.speedle.io/quick-start/). Use Go 1.26.10 or Go 1.27.3 (or a newer patch on the same release branch), Bash, curl and Python 3. Run each terminal from the repository root. Use a fresh policy file for this page; reset it only after stopping both services.

Initialize an empty policy file:


```bash
printf '{}\n' > docs-policies.json
```

> **macOS:** `/usr/sbin/spctl` is Apple's Gatekeeper tool and may be selected when you run a bare `spctl` command. Call Speedle's CLI by its full path, or use `./spctl` from the directory containing it; the examples below use `./bin/spctl`. Run `command -v spctl` to check which executable your shell selects. If the release you download includes a `speedle-spctl_<os>_<arch>` asset, it is the same CLI under a name that does not collide with Apple's tool.

In terminal one, start PMS and leave it running:


```bash
./bin/speedle-pms --store-type file --filestore-loc ./docs-policies.json --endpoint 127.0.0.1:6733 --grpc-endpoint 127.0.0.1:0 --insecure=true
```

In terminal two, start ADS and leave it running:


```bash
./bin/speedle-ads --store-type file --filestore-loc ./docs-policies.json --endpoint 127.0.0.1:6734 --grpc-endpoint 127.0.0.1:0 --insecure=true
```

Run the remaining commands in a third terminal. PMS and ADS share the file; watch propagates changes asynchronously. Confirm the intended update has reached ADS before relying on it. `--insecure=true` is only for this loopback example; see [security](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/security/) for production connections. Explicit PMS addresses avoid changing `~/.spctlconfig`. Stop both server terminals with Ctrl-C when finished.


### Manage services and policies with spctl

Run this sequence against a fresh store. IDs come from the live query responses; they are not fixed values copied from an older run. Deletion happens after all operations that need the service.


```bash
./bin/spctl --pms-endpoint http://127.0.0.1:6733/policy-mgmt/v1/ create service test
./bin/spctl --pms-endpoint http://127.0.0.1:6733/policy-mgmt/v1/ get service test
./bin/spctl --pms-endpoint http://127.0.0.1:6733/policy-mgmt/v1/ get service --all
./bin/spctl --pms-endpoint http://127.0.0.1:6733/policy-mgmt/v1/ create policy policy1 -c "grant user alan read book" --service-name test
policy_id=$(./bin/spctl --pms-endpoint http://127.0.0.1:6733/policy-mgmt/v1/ get policy --all --service-name test | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(next(p["id"] for p in json.load(sys.stdin) if p.get("name")=="policy1"))')
./bin/spctl --pms-endpoint http://127.0.0.1:6733/policy-mgmt/v1/ get policy "$policy_id" --service-name test
./bin/spctl --pms-endpoint http://127.0.0.1:6733/policy-mgmt/v1/ create rolepolicy rolepolicy01 -c "grant user alan manager on res1" --service-name test
role_policy_id=$(./bin/spctl --pms-endpoint http://127.0.0.1:6733/policy-mgmt/v1/ get rolepolicy --all --service-name test | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(next(p["id"] for p in json.load(sys.stdin) if p.get("name")=="rolepolicy01"))')
./bin/spctl --pms-endpoint http://127.0.0.1:6733/policy-mgmt/v1/ get rolepolicy "$role_policy_id" --service-name test
./bin/spctl --pms-endpoint http://127.0.0.1:6733/policy-mgmt/v1/ delete policy "$policy_id" --service-name test
./bin/spctl --pms-endpoint http://127.0.0.1:6733/policy-mgmt/v1/ delete rolepolicy "$role_policy_id" --service-name test
./bin/spctl --pms-endpoint http://127.0.0.1:6733/policy-mgmt/v1/ delete service test
```


### Speedle Cloud

Speedle Cloud sign-in opens soon. When API tokens become available, `spctl` can manage Cloud services and policies through the same commands used with a self-hosted PMS. Use the management endpoint:

```text
https://cloud.speedle.io/policy-mgmt/v1
```

Choose an API token with the scopes required by your commands. `pms:read` covers `get` and `discover` reads; `pms:write` covers `create`, `delete` and discovery resets. A token that only has ADS scopes cannot manage policies and is rejected with `403 insufficient_scope`.

Pass the endpoint as a global flag and read the token from `SPCTL_TOKEN`. In an interactive shell, this keeps the secret out of command arguments and shell history:

```bash
read -rsp 'API token: ' SPCTL_TOKEN; echo
export SPCTL_TOKEN
./bin/spctl --pms-endpoint https://cloud.speedle.io/policy-mgmt/v1 get service --all
unset SPCTL_TOKEN
```

The `--token` flag remains available for compatibility, but the environment variable avoids exposing the token through command arguments. Every global flag also has an environment variable: prefix `SPCTL_`, uppercase the flag name and replace hyphens with underscores. For example, `SPCTL_PMS_ENDPOINT` sets `pms-endpoint` and `SPCTL_SKIPVERIFY` sets `skipverify`.

For a saved configuration, use `~/.speedle`. Its format is one `name=value` pair per line, with the same flag names as the command line:

```ini
pms-endpoint=https://cloud.speedle.io/policy-mgmt/v1
token=<api-token>
```

Create or update this file without putting the token in command arguments:

```bash
read -rsp 'API token: ' SPCTL_TOKEN; echo
printf '%s\n' "$SPCTL_TOKEN" | ./bin/spctl config token --stdin
unset SPCTL_TOKEN
```

`spctl config token --stdin` writes `~/.speedle` with mode `0600`. When editing the file manually, create it with `install -m 600 /dev/null ~/.speedle` or run `chmod 0600 ~/.speedle` afterwards. `spctl` warns on standard error if it reads a token from a file whose permissions allow group or other access. `spctl config --list` masks a configured token as `********`.

Explicit command-line flags override environment variables, which override both configuration files. Within the files, `~/.speedle` overrides `~/.spctlconfig`. Setting a non-token key with `spctl config` writes it to `~/.spctlconfig` and removes any shadowing copy from `~/.speedle`.

The token is sent as an `Authorization: Bearer` credential only over HTTPS with certificate verification enabled. Plain HTTP is allowed with a token only for a loopback host such as `127.0.0.1`, `::1` or `localhost`; `spctl` rejects remote HTTP endpoints and HTTPS-to-HTTP downgrade redirects before sending the credential. It also refuses to send a token with `--skipverify=true`; use `--cacert` to trust a private or self-signed certificate authority instead. Tokens are not included in normal command output or error messages.

Cloud errors produce a non-zero exit status. Check the token after a `401`, and its scopes after a `403 insufficient_scope`. A `404` identifies a missing resource, while `409 service_exists` and `409 policy_exists` identify duplicates. For `429`, honor the returned `Retry-After` value and use bounded backoff. Daily or policy quota errors require waiting for the reset or reducing usage; do not retry them in a tight loop.


### Other interfaces

The [PMS REST API](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/api/management_api/) uses JSON and returns flat policy objects with string IDs. Go applications can call the [PMS interfaces](https://github.com/teramoby/speedle-plus/tree/master/api/pms) directly; gRPC clients use the [published PMS proto](https://engine.speedle.io/protobuf/pms.proto). Apply [transport and caller access controls](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/security/) to administrative operations.

## Global Policy

Source: https://engine.speedle.io/docs/pms/global-policy/

### When should a role be global?

Ordinary roles are scoped to a service. When several services share a role assignment, define the assignment in the specially named `global` service and use that role in each service's own authorization policies.

Only global **role policies** are supported. A global role assignment does not itself grant every operation; each ordinary service still defines its permissions. Global authorization policies are not supported.

### Before running the examples

Build `./bin/spctl`, `./bin/speedle-pms` and `./bin/speedle-ads` using the [quick start](https://engine.speedle.io/quick-start/). Use Go 1.26.10 or Go 1.27.3 (or a newer patch on the same release branch), Bash, curl and Python 3. Run each terminal from the repository root. Use a fresh policy file for this page; reset it only after stopping both services.

Initialize an empty policy file:


```bash
printf '{}\n' > docs-policies.json
```

In terminal one, start PMS and leave it running:


```bash
./bin/speedle-pms --store-type file --filestore-loc ./docs-policies.json --endpoint 127.0.0.1:6733 --grpc-endpoint 127.0.0.1:0 --insecure=true
```

In terminal two, start ADS and leave it running:


```bash
./bin/speedle-ads --store-type file --filestore-loc ./docs-policies.json --endpoint 127.0.0.1:6734 --grpc-endpoint 127.0.0.1:0 --insecure=true
```

Run the remaining commands in a third terminal. PMS and ADS share the file; watch propagates changes asynchronously. Confirm the intended update has reached ADS before relying on it. `--insecure=true` is only for this loopback example; see [security](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/security/) for production connections. Explicit PMS addresses avoid changing `~/.spctlconfig`. Stop both server terminals with Ctrl-C when finished.


### Create a global role and a local permission


```bash
./bin/spctl --pms-endpoint http://127.0.0.1:6733/policy-mgmt/v1/ create service global
./bin/spctl --pms-endpoint http://127.0.0.1:6733/policy-mgmt/v1/ create rolepolicy -c "grant user Emma AdminRole" --service-name global
./bin/spctl --pms-endpoint http://127.0.0.1:6733/policy-mgmt/v1/ create service library
./bin/spctl --pms-endpoint http://127.0.0.1:6733/policy-mgmt/v1/ create policy -c "grant role AdminRole borrow books" --service-name library
```


`global` must use exactly that service name. `library` is created before its policy. Both are managed through normal service APIs.

### Check the result

Emma is allowed through `AdminRole`; Bob is denied.


```bash
curl --fail --silent --show-error -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"subject":{"principals":[{"type":"user","name":"Emma"}]},"serviceName":"library","resource":"books","action":"borrow"}' \
  http://127.0.0.1:6734/authz-check/v1/is-allowed
```



```bash
curl --fail --silent --show-error -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"subject":{"principals":[{"type":"user","name":"Bob"}]},"serviceName":"library","resource":"books","action":"borrow"}' \
  http://127.0.0.1:6734/authz-check/v1/is-allowed
```


A resource-scoped global role policy applies only to its resource scope. Keep cross-service role assignments under review, especially when identities span [different domains](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/idd/).

## Policy Discovery

Source: https://engine.speedle.io/docs/pms/discover/

### What discovery does

Discovery records requests and returns `allowed=true` with reason 5 for a successful recording operation. It does not prove that an existing policy authorized the operation. Use it only in an isolated test environment, review generated grants, and restore normal `is-allowed` enforcement afterwards. Assertion or storage errors must still be handled; never treat an error as an authorization grant.

### Start a reproducible local example

Build the binaries using [Quick Start](https://engine.speedle.io/quick-start/), then run all terminals from the checkout root. Use a fresh file and stop previous page fixtures before starting.


```bash
printf '{}\n' > docs-policies.json
```

In terminal one:


```bash
./bin/speedle-pms --store-type file --filestore-loc ./docs-policies.json --endpoint 127.0.0.1:6733 --insecure=true
```

In terminal two:


```bash
./bin/speedle-ads --store-type file --filestore-loc ./docs-policies.json --endpoint 127.0.0.1:6734 --insecure=true
```

Keep both running. In terminal three, record one request:


```bash
curl --fail --silent --show-error -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"subject":{"principals":[{"type":"user","name":"alice"}]},"serviceName":"observed","resource":"book","action":"read"}' \
  http://127.0.0.1:6734/authz-check/v1/discover
```

Inspect the captured request, then generate a proposed service definition:


```bash
./bin/spctl --pms-endpoint http://127.0.0.1:6733/policy-mgmt/v1/ discover request --service-name observed
```

```bash
./bin/spctl --pms-endpoint http://127.0.0.1:6733/policy-mgmt/v1/ discover policy --service-name observed > discovered-service.json
```

Review `discovered-service.json`, including generated roles, identity domains and resources. The fresh example has no existing service named `observed`, so it can be imported directly; for an existing service, reconcile its policies rather than blindly recreating it.


```bash
./bin/spctl --pms-endpoint http://127.0.0.1:6733/policy-mgmt/v1/ create service --json-file discovered-service.json
```

### Restore and verify normal enforcement

Call `is-allowed` again. Alice should be allowed after ADS has loaded the policy update; Bob must still be denied:


```bash
curl --fail --silent --show-error -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"subject":{"principals":[{"type":"user","name":"alice"}]},"serviceName":"observed","resource":"book","action":"read"}' \
  http://127.0.0.1:6734/authz-check/v1/is-allowed
```

```bash
curl --fail --silent --show-error -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"subject":{"principals":[{"type":"user","name":"bob"}]},"serviceName":"observed","resource":"book","action":"read"}' \
  http://127.0.0.1:6734/authz-check/v1/is-allowed
```

Stop both services with Ctrl+C. For gRPC use `Discover`/`IsAllowed` on the generated client; embedded Go uses `evaluator.Discover(ctx)`/`evaluator.IsAllowed(ctx)`. For CLI options, run `./bin/spctl discover --help`. Do not leave a real application pointing at `/discover`.

## Policy Diagnosis

Source: https://engine.speedle.io/docs/pms/diagnosis/

### What does diagnosis show?

`Diagnose` explains an authorization evaluation: decision, reason, effective roles, attributes, and the policies examined. It accepts the same request context as `IsAllowed`; REST uses `/authz-check/v1/diagnose`, and both Go/gRPC use `Diagnose`.

Diagnosis exposes policy definitions and request context. Restrict it to trusted operators using the [API security controls](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/security/); it is not a public debugging endpoint.

### Before running the examples

Build `./bin/spctl`, `./bin/speedle-pms` and `./bin/speedle-ads` using the [quick start](https://engine.speedle.io/quick-start/). Use Go 1.26.10 or Go 1.27.3 (or a newer patch on the same release branch), Bash, curl and Python 3. Run each terminal from the repository root. Use a fresh policy file for this page; reset it only after stopping both services.

Initialize an empty policy file:


```bash
printf '{}\n' > docs-policies.json
```

In terminal one, start PMS and leave it running:


```bash
./bin/speedle-pms --store-type file --filestore-loc ./docs-policies.json --endpoint 127.0.0.1:6733 --grpc-endpoint 127.0.0.1:0 --insecure=true
```

In terminal two, start ADS and leave it running:


```bash
./bin/speedle-ads --store-type file --filestore-loc ./docs-policies.json --endpoint 127.0.0.1:6734 --grpc-endpoint 127.0.0.1:0 --insecure=true
```

Run the remaining commands in a third terminal. PMS and ADS share the file; watch propagates changes asynchronously. Confirm the intended update has reached ADS before relying on it. `--insecure=true` is only for this loopback example; see [security](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/security/) for production connections. Explicit PMS addresses avoid changing `~/.spctlconfig`. Stop both server terminals with Ctrl-C when finished.


### Create the example policies

The [fixture](https://github.com/teramoby/speedle-plus/blob/master/website/tests/examples/diagnosis.json) grants `get` under `^/api/v1/example/.*$` but explicitly denies `/api/v1/example/res1` for `user1`.


```bash
./bin/spctl --pms-endpoint http://127.0.0.1:6733/policy-mgmt/v1/ create service --json-file website/tests/examples/diagnosis.json
```


### Compare decision and diagnosis


```bash
curl --fail --silent --show-error -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"subject":{"principals":[{"type":"user","name":"user1"}]},"serviceName":"srv1","resource":"/api/v1/example/res1","action":"get"}' \
  http://127.0.0.1:6734/authz-check/v1/is-allowed
```


Expected: `allowed=false`, `reason=1` (explicit deny).


```bash
curl --fail --silent --show-error -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"subject":{"principals":[{"type":"user","name":"user1"}]},"serviceName":"srv1","resource":"/api/v1/example/res1","action":"get"}' \
  http://127.0.0.1:6734/authz-check/v1/diagnose
```


The diagnostic response uses `allowed` as a Boolean, `reason` as a string such as `DENY_POLICY_FOUND`, and `attributes` as an object. `request_month` is a numeric month. `requestContext.subject.principals` is an array; authorization policies contain a two-dimensional `principals` array representing OR-of-AND principal groups.

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `requestContext` | The request used in evaluation; REST attributes remain a typed array here |
| `attributes` | Available request and built-in attributes, keyed by name |
| `grantedRoles` | Effective roles, when present |
| `rolePolicies`, `policies` | Evaluated role and authorization policy details, when present |
| `condition` | Expression and result; may be empty for unconditional policies |

Policy status values are `takeEffect`, `conditionFailed` and `ignored`. `ignored` means the final result was already determined, so that policy did not need evaluation. Ordering can vary; inspect IDs and status rather than matching a historical response verbatim. See the [decision schema](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/api/decision_api/) for the complete response contract.

## Custom Function

Source: https://engine.speedle.io/docs/custom-function/

### Why use a custom function?

SPDL conditions can call a configured function when built-in operators or functions do not express the required rule. Speedle calls its REST endpoint with `POST {"params":[...]}` and expects `{"result":...}` or `{"error":"..."}`. Parameter order/types and the result type must match the condition. Function failures are evaluation errors; applications must fail closed.

### Start the local example

This example accepts numeric values from 100 to 50000. Wrong parameter types or an empty parameter list return an HTTP error. It uses plaintext only on a loopback IP; use TLS for other interfaces.

Start it in a separate terminal:


```bash
go run ./website/tests/examples/custom-function
```



```go
package main

import (
	"encoding/json"
	"flag"
	"log"
	"net"
	"net/http"
	"time"
)

type request struct {
	Params []interface{} `json:"params"`
}
type response struct {
	Result interface{} `json:"result,omitempty"`
	Error  string      `json:"error,omitempty"`
}

func isValid(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
	send := func(status int, value response) {
		w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
		w.WriteHeader(status)
		_ = json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(value)
	}
	if r.Method != http.MethodPost {
		w.Header().Set("Allow", "POST")
		send(405, response{Error: "POST required"})
		return
	}
	decoder := json.NewDecoder(http.MaxBytesReader(w, r.Body, 1<<20))
	decoder.DisallowUnknownFields()
	var input request
	if err := decoder.Decode(&input); err != nil || len(input.Params) == 0 {
		send(400, response{Error: "params must contain at least one number"})
		return
	}
	valid := true
	for _, param := range input.Params {
		value, ok := param.(float64)
		if !ok {
			send(400, response{Error: "all params must be numbers"})
			return
		}
		if value < 100 || value > 50000 {
			valid = false
		}
	}
	send(200, response{Result: valid})
}
func main() {
	listen := flag.String("listen", "127.0.0.1:23456", "Function listen address")
	cert := flag.String("cert", "", "TLS server certificate")
	key := flag.String("key", "", "TLS server key")
	flag.Parse()
	if (*cert == "") != (*key == "") {
		log.Fatal("provide both --cert and --key")
	}
	mux := http.NewServeMux()
	mux.HandleFunc("/func/isValid", isValid)
	server := &http.Server{Addr: *listen, Handler: mux, ReadHeaderTimeout: 5 * time.Second, ReadTimeout: 10 * time.Second, WriteTimeout: 10 * time.Second}
	if *cert != "" {
		log.Fatal(server.ListenAndServeTLS(*cert, *key))
	}
	host, _, err := net.SplitHostPort(*listen)
	if err != nil || !net.ParseIP(host).IsLoopback() {
		log.Fatal("plaintext examples require a loopback IP; provide TLS certificates for other addresses")
	}
	log.Fatal(server.ListenAndServe())
}
```


### Before running the examples

Build `./bin/spctl`, `./bin/speedle-pms` and `./bin/speedle-ads` using the [quick start](https://engine.speedle.io/quick-start/). Use Go 1.26.10 or Go 1.27.3 (or a newer patch on the same release branch), Bash, curl and Python 3. Run each terminal from the repository root. Use a fresh policy file for this page; reset it only after stopping both services.

Initialize an empty policy file:


```bash

```

In terminal one, start PMS and leave it running:


