
### Production deployments

Use durable policy storage, pin container image digests to the release version you deploy (a release retry can republish a version tag), protect management and decision endpoints, and configure TLS/mTLS for clients and the policy backend. [Pluggable Storage](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/store/) documents the current store configuration; [Security](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/security/) covers current transport flags. Size and operate the etcd deployment using the current etcd documentation, not the retired etcd-operator example.

The repository contains historical Helm/Kubernetes examples. The old Helm 2 `helm install -n ...`, `stable/etcd-operator`, `apps/v1beta2`, and `r.authz.fun` image instructions are not the deployment flow above. Container pulls, cluster admission, registry access, storage and rollout depend on your environment; validate them in your target cluster before production use.

## Speedle embedded mode

Source: https://engine.speedle.io/docs/deployment-embeded/

### What is embedded mode?

Embedded mode runs the Speedle policy decision engine inside your Go application. Call the evaluator directly without starting PMS or ADS servers. Your application authenticates users and supplies the subject, resource and action for each decision.

To try basic policies before writing code, open the [Playground](https://engine.speedle.io/playground/). To run Speedle as standalone services, follow [Quick Start](https://engine.speedle.io/quick-start/).

### Prerequisites

Use Linux or macOS with a shell and **Go 1.26.10 or Go 1.27.3** (or a newer patch on the same release branch), matching [Quick Start](https://engine.speedle.io/quick-start/). This walkthrough uses Go modules and the published **Speedle v1.6.0** release. Go 1.27.3 is the recommended toolchain; the example is verified with Go 1.26.10 and Go 1.27.3.

Install Go using the [official installation instructions](https://go.dev/doc/install), then check your version:


```bash
go version
```

Go configures `GOROOT` and its default `GOPATH` automatically; no custom values are needed.

### Create an application module

Start in a writable directory outside the Speedle source checkout. Use a new directory for this walkthrough:


```bash
mkdir speedle-embedded-demo
cd speedle-embedded-demo
go mod init example.com/speedle-embedded-demo
go get github.com/teramoby/speedle-plus/pkg/eval@v1.6.0
```

In an existing Go module, run only the final `go get` command from that module's directory.

Here, `go get` adds a versioned **library dependency** to `go.mod` and `go.sum`; it does not install a program. This differs from Quick Start, which uses `git clone` and `go build` to build the standalone service executables. Both use Go modules. Keep `go.mod` and `go.sum` in version control.

### Create a policy file

In `speedle-embedded-demo`, save this content as `policies.spdl`. It grants `alice` permission to `get` resource `res1` in service `mysvc`:


```ini
[service.mysvc]
[policy]
grant user alice get res1
```

The `eval.NewFromFile` constructor loads a local file containing SPDL or JSON policies. This walkthrough uses SPDL.

### Initialize the evaluator and request decisions

Save the following complete program as `main.go` in the same directory:


```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"log"

	"github.com/teramoby/speedle-plus/api/ads"
	"github.com/teramoby/speedle-plus/pkg/eval"
	_ "github.com/teramoby/speedle-plus/pkg/store/file"
)

func main() {
	evaluator, err := eval.NewFromFile("./policies.spdl", false)
	if err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}

	for _, user := range []string{"alice", "bob"} {
		allowed, _, err := evaluator.IsAllowed(ads.RequestContext{
			Subject: &ads.Subject{
				Principals: []*ads.Principal{{Type: ads.PRINCIPAL_TYPE_USER, Name: user}},
			},
			ServiceName: "mysvc",
			Resource:    "res1",
			Action:      "get",
		})
		if err != nil {
			log.Fatal(err)
		}
		fmt.Printf("%s allowed=%t\n", user, allowed)
	}
}
```

The blank import `_ "github.com/teramoby/speedle-plus/pkg/store/file"` registers the file-store driver. Omitting it causes an `unknown store type "file"` error.

`eval.NewFromFile(loc, isWatch)` returns an `ads.PolicyEvaluator` and an error. Check the error before using the evaluator. With `isWatch=false`, policies are loaded once; setting it to `true` enables file watching for a long-running application.

Call `evaluator.IsAllowed(ctx)` on that instance. Its `ads.RequestContext` contains the subject's principals, `ServiceName`, `Resource`, `Action` and optional `Attributes`. It returns `(allowed bool, reason ads.Reason, err error)`. An evaluation error must be handled separately from a successful `allowed=false` decision.

### Build and run

From `speedle-embedded-demo`, resolve dependencies and build your application:


```bash
go mod tidy
go build -o ./bin/embedded-demo .
```

Run it from the same directory so that `./policies.spdl` resolves correctly:


```bash
./bin/embedded-demo
```

The decision output is:

```text
alice allowed=true
bob allowed=false
```

`alice` matches the grant; `bob` has no matching grant and is denied. No network services or database are needed for this example.

## Pluggable Storage

Source: https://engine.speedle.io/docs/store/

### Built-in stores and extension contracts

The standalone binaries register file, etcd, MongoDB and MySQL implementations under `pkg/store`. Availability does not mean identical operational guarantees; review backend authentication, persistence, transaction and watch behavior for your deployment. The configuration below illustrates property names; running etcd/MongoDB deployments is outside this local example.

A full backend implements [pms.PolicyStoreManager](https://github.com/teramoby/speedle-plus/blob/master/api/pms/interface.go): service, authorization-policy, role-policy and function management, snapshot reads and watch/stop. ADS accepts the narrower `PolicyStoreManagerADS` read/watch interface. Check the actual interfaces when implementing a backend, rather than copying a partial historical method list.

For deployment walkthroughs, see [MySQL Setup](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/store/mysql/),
[etcd Setup](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/store/etcd/) and [MongoDB Setup](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/store/mongodb/).

### Store failures and cached authorization

File, etcd, MySQL and MongoDB use the same ADS failure policy. The default
`storeFailureGracePeriod` is `"0s"`: once a store failure is detected, authorization
returns `allowed:false` and an evaluation error. ADS stays running and retries.
A readable connection alone does not restore authorization; a successful complete
snapshot reload is required. With watching enabled, a failed subscription must
be re-established first; successful data reads while watch is broken do not reset
the failure/grace deadline. A deleted file is retried instead of terminating ADS.

Deployments that explicitly accept delayed revocation can set a finite duration,
for example `"storeFailureGracePeriod": "5s"` at the top level of the ADS JSON
configuration. The equivalent flag is `--store-failure-grace-period=5s`, and the
environment variable is `SPDL_STORE_FAILURE_GRACE_PERIOD`. The usual flag →
environment → file → default precedence applies. Repeated failures do not extend
the deadline. Within the grace period decisions use the last complete snapshot,
so revocations cannot take effect until synchronization recovers. Partial-cache
failures and evaluation panics never receive a grace period.

Built-in stores have lightweight health probes, checked about once per second
with a one-second probe timeout. Watches may report failure sooner; in-flight
store reads also have their backend timeouts. Failure detection and ordinary
policy propagation are asynchronous, not immediate revocation guarantees.
With `enableWatch:false`, requests still check store health; ordinary policy
updates require an explicit refresh. After an outage, recovery loads a complete
snapshot even in that mode. An initial load failure cannot use a grace period.
Custom stores can implement `pms.StoreHealthChecker` and publish
`pms.STORE_UNAVAILABLE` events to participate in the same failure policy.

File-store PMS writes publish a fully serialized, synced temporary file with a
same-directory atomic rename. Independent ADS readers therefore see a complete
old or new snapshot. The writer needs write access to the parent directory;
existing permission bits and configured symlinks are preserved. The replacement
file is created by the writer account, so configure directory group/ACL inheritance
for separate PMS/ADS users. Containers must share the policy directory so
replacements are visible to both services. Directly created new policy files use mode 0600;
the normal file-store builder continues to initialize missing stores as before.

### MySQL 8.4 policy store

Follow the [step-by-step MySQL setup guide](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/store/mysql/) to create a
database, configure separate PMS/ADS accounts, and verify policy synchronization.

The `mysql` backend implements the complete policy-store interface for PMS and ADS. Discover request collection and policy generation are not supported. It uses the pure-Go `go-sql-driver/mysql` driver; the database must already exist.

```json
{
  "storeConfig": {
    "storeType": "mysql",
    "storeProps": {
      "MySQLDSN": "speedle:replace-me@tcp(db.example.com:3306)/speedle?tls=true",
      "MySQLInitSchema": true,
      "MySQLPollInterval": "1s",
      "MySQLQueryTimeout": "10s"
    }
  },
  "enableWatch": true
}
```

| Property | Flag | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MySQLDSN` | `--mysqlstore-dsn` | Required, including database name |
| `MySQLInitSchema` | `--mysqlstore-init-schema` | `true` |
| `MySQLPollInterval` | `--mysqlstore-poll-interval` | `1s` |
| `MySQLQueryTimeout` | `--mysqlstore-query-timeout` | `10s` |

Environment variables use the same mapping, for example `SPDL_MYSQLSTORE_DSN`. Durations must be positive strings; `MySQLInitSchema` accepts a JSON boolean or a boolean string. Explicit flags override nonempty environment variables, then configuration-file values, then defaults. For embedded use, import `pkg/store/mysql`, pass these properties directly to `store.NewStore`, and close the returned `*mysql.Store` when finished. An evaluator created through `eval.NewFromConfig` can be closed through `io.Closer`; closing an evaluator also closes a closable supplied store.

#### Schema and provisioning

One database is one policy store, using five fixed InnoDB tables: `speedle_services`, `speedle_policies`, `speedle_role_policies`, `speedle_functions`, and `speedle_store_meta`. Complex arrays and metadata use JSON columns. Policy tables reference the service with cascading deletion. Service/function names and policy IDs use case-sensitive, non-padding comparisons and support up to 255 Unicode characters; policy names need not be unique.

By default, startup creates missing tables using [schema.sql](https://github.com/teramoby/speedle-plus/blob/master/pkg/store/mysql/schema.sql). It does not create a database or alter an existing schema. For a prebuilt deployment, run that same SQL against the selected database using a provisioning account, then set `MySQLInitSchema` to `false`. Startup checks the schema version, required columns and InnoDB engines. An unsupported schema version fails startup; future upgrades require an explicit migration.

Provisioning requires table-creation and initialization privileges. With a prebuilt schema, the PMS account needs `SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, and `DELETE` on the policy database; ADS can use a separate account with only `SELECT` and automatic schema creation disabled. Use driver DSN TLS options for remote databases. Do not put production passwords in committed configuration or command-line history.

#### Transactions, synchronization and recovery

Each write locks the single revision row and commits data changes together with a revision increment. This serializes policy writes across PMS instances. Service creation with nested policies, cascading deletion, and whole-store replacement are atomic. Import preserves supplied policy IDs and assigns IDs where absent. Snapshot reads use one repeatable-read transaction.

With `enableWatch`, ADS polls the revision and receives a complete consistent snapshot when it changes. Startup also sends a snapshot to cover updates between the initial read and watch registration. Propagation is asynchronous, normally within a polling interval plus query/cache-rebuild time. During a database outage ADS retains its data but suspends cached authorization by default, retries reads, and reloads a complete snapshot before resuming. The shared failure/grace policy above applies. Changes made directly in SQL without incrementing the revision are not discovered automatically; use PMS or the store interface for policy writes.

The operation timeout also bounds connection-pool waits and transaction lock waits. Failed writes are rolled back; a connection loss during commit can leave the outcome uncertain, so callers should inspect stored state before retrying a non-idempotent create. `StopWatch` and `Close` are idempotent and release watch resources; `Close` also closes the connection pool.

### Implement and register a builder

A [store.StoreBuilder](https://github.com/teramoby/speedle-plus/blob/master/pkg/store/store.go) provides `NewStore(map[string]interface{}) (pms.PolicyStoreManager, error)` and `GetStoreParams() map[string]string`. The latter maps flag names to configuration property names. Register a unique store type in `init()` or before calling `store.NewStore`; duplicate registration is an error.

This complete example delegates to the existing file backend to demonstrate the factory contract. It does not claim to implement a new database:


```bash
go run ./website/tests/examples/store
```



```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"github.com/teramoby/speedle-plus/pkg/store"
	"github.com/teramoby/speedle-plus/pkg/store/file"
	"log"
	"os"
	"path/filepath"
)

// This example delegates to the file backend to demonstrate registration.
// A new backend must implement the complete PolicyStoreManager contract.
type Builder struct{ file.FileStoreBuilder }

func main() {
	dir, err := os.MkdirTemp("", "speedle-store-example-")
	if err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
	defer os.RemoveAll(dir)
	store.Register("myfile", Builder{})
	policies, err := store.NewStore("myfile", map[string]interface{}{"FileLocation": filepath.Join(dir, "policies.json")})
	if err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
	snapshot, err := policies.ReadPolicyStore()
	if err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
	fmt.Printf("Registered myfile store; services=%d\n", len(snapshot.Services))
}
```


### Merge configuration correctly

For standalone commands, explicit flags override nonempty environment variables, then configuration-file properties, then defaults. Convert the flag name by adding `SPDL_`, replacing `-` with `_`, and uppercasing: `etcdstore-endpoint` becomes `SPDL_ETCDSTORE_ENDPOINT`. Values may arrive as strings from flags/env or typed JSON values; validate and convert deliberately.

```json
{
  "storeConfig": {
    "storeType": "etcd",
    "storeProps": {
      "EtcdEndpoint": "localhost:2379",
      "EtcdKeyPrefix": "/speedle_ps/",
      "IsEmbeddedEtcd": true,
      "EmbeddedEtcdDataDir": "./speedle.etcd"
    }
  },
  "enableWatch": true
}
```

Define custom flags with `pflag` before parsing and return their flag-to-property mapping from `GetStoreParams`. Embedded callers pass the configuration map directly to `store.NewStore`/`eval.NewFromConfig`; the factory alone does not read command-line or environment configuration.

### Link the backend and handle updates

Use side-effect imports in both standalone binaries (or your embedded application) when registration happens in `init()`:

```go
import (
    _ "github.com/teramoby/speedle-plus/pkg/store/etcd"
    _ "github.com/teramoby/speedle-plus/pkg/store/file"
    _ "github.com/teramoby/speedle-plus/pkg/store/mongodb"
    _ "github.com/teramoby/speedle-plus/pkg/store/mysql"
)
```

Implement `Watch()` so it returns the correct snapshot/change events through `pms.StorageChangeChannel`; support `StopWatch()` without leaking watch resources. ADS updates its runtime cache asynchronously. Test missed/disconnected watches, recovery, failure during a write, and concurrent readers; do not promise instantaneous propagation simply because the backend supports watch.

## MySQL Setup

Source: https://engine.speedle.io/docs/store/mysql/

This guide uses **MySQL 8.4 LTS** and two native Speedle processes: PMS writes
policies, and ADS reads the same database with a separate read-only account.
The local example uses Docker and plain HTTP on loopback. For a remote deployment,
use your existing MySQL server and the [Security guide](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/security/).

### 1. Build Speedle with the MySQL backend

Install Git, Bash, curl, Docker and a supported Go toolchain (Go 1.26.10 or
Go 1.27.3). Docker must be running. Build from current source so both binaries
contain the `mysql` store; an older installed release may not contain it.


```bash
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/teramoby/speedle-plus.git
cd speedle-plus
mkdir -p bin
go build -o ./bin/ ./cmd/spctl ./cmd/speedle-pms ./cmd/speedle-ads
```

Run the remaining commands from this `speedle-plus` directory. Keep ports 3306,
6733 and 6734 free, or change the corresponding addresses in every command and
configuration below.

### 2. Start MySQL 8.4

The fixed passwords below are **local demo credentials**. Use your own credentials
and secret delivery mechanism when deploying. The named Docker volume preserves
the database when this container is stopped or recreated.


```bash
docker run --name speedle-mysql --detach \
  --publish 127.0.0.1:3306:3306 \
  --volume speedle-mysql-data:/var/lib/mysql \
  --env MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=SpeedleDemoRoot84 \
  mysql:8.4
```

Wait for initialization to finish:


```bash
until docker exec speedle-mysql mysqladmin ping \
  --host=127.0.0.1 --user=root --password=SpeedleDemoRoot84 --silent
do
  sleep 1
done
```

If you already have MySQL 8.4, skip these Docker commands and run the SQL in the
next step using your database administrator's client. The Docker image initializes
credentials only when its data directory is empty; changing an environment
variable does not reset a password in an existing volume.

### 3. Create the database and service accounts

Speedle creates tables by default, but **does not create the database**. Use an
administrator to create `speedle` and two accounts:


```bash
docker exec -i speedle-mysql mysql --user=root --password=SpeedleDemoRoot84 <<'SQL'
CREATE DATABASE speedle CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_0900_bin;
CREATE USER 'speedle_pms'@'%' IDENTIFIED BY 'SpeedleDemoPms84';
CREATE USER 'speedle_ads'@'%' IDENTIFIED BY 'SpeedleDemoAds84';
GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, CREATE, REFERENCES ON speedle.* TO 'speedle_pms'@'%';
GRANT SELECT ON speedle.* TO 'speedle_ads'@'%';
SQL
```

PMS needs `CREATE` and `REFERENCES` for automatic schema initialization, plus
`SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE` and `DELETE` for policy management. ADS needs only
`SELECT` and must disable automatic schema initialization. The `%` account host
allows connections from the host through Docker; restrict account hosts to your
actual PMS/ADS machines for a remote deployment.

### 4. Write the PMS and ADS configuration files

Both DSNs must select the **same server and database**. A DSN follows the driver
syntax `user:password@tcp(host:port)/database`.


```bash
mkdir -p mysql-demo
cat > mysql-demo/pms.json <<'JSON'
{
  "storeConfig": {
    "storeType": "mysql",
    "storeProps": {
      "MySQLDSN": "speedle_pms:SpeedleDemoPms84@tcp(127.0.0.1:3306)/speedle",
      "MySQLInitSchema": true,
      "MySQLPollInterval": "1s",
      "MySQLQueryTimeout": "10s"
    }
  }
}
JSON
cat > mysql-demo/ads.json <<'JSON'
{
  "storeConfig": {
    "storeType": "mysql",
    "storeProps": {
      "MySQLDSN": "speedle_ads:SpeedleDemoAds84@tcp(127.0.0.1:3306)/speedle",
      "MySQLInitSchema": false,
      "MySQLPollInterval": "1s",
      "MySQLQueryTimeout": "10s"
    }
  },
  "enableWatch": true
}
JSON
chmod 600 mysql-demo/pms.json mysql-demo/ads.json
```

`MySQLInitSchema: false` makes startup check the existing schema without executing
DDL. `enableWatch: true` lets ADS follow committed changes. Do not commit these
credential-bearing configuration files.

### 5. Start PMS, then ADS

In terminal A, start PMS first so it can create the tables:


```bash
./bin/speedle-pms --config-file mysql-demo/pms.json --endpoint 127.0.0.1:6733 --insecure=true
```

Leave PMS running. In terminal B, from the same checkout, confirm initialization:


```bash
docker exec speedle-mysql mysql --user=speedle_ads --password=SpeedleDemoAds84 speedle -e 'SHOW TABLES;'
```

You should see five tables:

| Table | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `speedle_services` | Services and service metadata |
| `speedle_policies` | Authorization policies |
| `speedle_role_policies` | Role policies |
| `speedle_functions` | Custom function definitions |
| `speedle_store_meta` | Schema version and committed policy revision |

Then start ADS in terminal B and leave it running:


```bash
./bin/speedle-ads --config-file mysql-demo/ads.json --endpoint 127.0.0.1:6734 --insecure=true
```

Wait for each service's REST listener to start before continuing. The gRPC servers
remain off unless you also pass `--grpc-endpoint`.

### 6. Create a policy and check authorization

In terminal C, create a service with a policy granting Alice permission to read
`book`:


```bash
curl -fsS -X POST http://127.0.0.1:6733/policy-mgmt/v1/service \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"mysql-demo","type":"application","policies":[{"name":"alice-read","effect":"grant","principals":[["user:alice"]],"permissions":[{"resource":"book","actions":["read"]}]}]}'
```

Allow up to a polling interval (1 second by default), plus query/cache rebuild
time, for ADS to load the change. Repeat the request if synchronization is still
in progress:


```bash
curl -fsS -X POST http://127.0.0.1:6734/authz-check/v1/is-allowed \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"subject":{"principals":[{"type":"user","name":"alice"}]},"serviceName":"mysql-demo","resource":"book","action":"read"}'
```

Expected response: `{"allowed":true,"reason":0}`. Bob has no matching grant:


```bash
curl -fsS -X POST http://127.0.0.1:6734/authz-check/v1/is-allowed \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"subject":{"principals":[{"type":"user","name":"bob"}]},"serviceName":"mysql-demo","resource":"book","action":"read"}'
```

Expected response: `{"allowed":false,"reason":3}`.

### 7. Verify automatic updates and persistence

Add an explicit deny for Alice through PMS, without restarting ADS:


```bash
curl -fsS -X POST http://127.0.0.1:6733/policy-mgmt/v1/service/mysql-demo/policy \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"alice-deny","effect":"deny","principals":[["user:alice"]],"permissions":[{"resource":"book","actions":["read"]}]}'
```

After synchronization, repeat Alice's request from step 6. It should now return
`{"allowed":false,"reason":1}`: the explicit deny takes priority. You can stop
PMS and ADS with Ctrl+C, restart them with the commands in step 5, and repeat the
same request. The stored policy and denial persist in MySQL.

Policy changes must go through PMS or the store interface so that data and the
revision advance in the same transaction. Direct SQL edits do not automatically
trigger an ADS reload. During a database outage, ADS stays running and retries synchronization but
defaults to `allowed:false` and an error once the failure is detected. A complete
snapshot must load successfully before authorization resumes. See the shared
[store failure and grace-period policy](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/store/#store-failures-and-cached-authorization).
Starting ADS still requires a reachable database.

### Pre-create the schema without runtime DDL privileges

As an alternative to automatic table creation, run the repository's
[schema.sql](https://github.com/teramoby/speedle-plus/blob/master/pkg/store/mysql/schema.sql)
with a provisioning account before starting either service:


```bash
docker exec -i speedle-mysql mysql --user=root --password=SpeedleDemoRoot84 speedle < pkg/store/mysql/schema.sql
```

Set `MySQLInitSchema` to `false` in **both** configuration files. If you followed
the demo above, remove the extra initialization privileges:


```bash
docker exec speedle-mysql mysql --user=root --password=SpeedleDemoRoot84 -e "REVOKE CREATE, REFERENCES ON speedle.* FROM 'speedle_pms'@'%';"
```

PMS then runs with `SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`; ADS stays read-only.
Restart both services after changing their configuration. Schema initialization
does not migrate existing tables; unsupported schema versions fail startup.

### Configuration reference and troubleshooting

| Property | Flag | Environment variable | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `MySQLDSN` | `--mysqlstore-dsn` | `SPDL_MYSQLSTORE_DSN` | Required, including database name |
| `MySQLInitSchema` | `--mysqlstore-init-schema` | `SPDL_MYSQLSTORE_INIT_SCHEMA` | `true` |
| `MySQLPollInterval` | `--mysqlstore-poll-interval` | `SPDL_MYSQLSTORE_POLL_INTERVAL` | `1s` |
| `MySQLQueryTimeout` | `--mysqlstore-query-timeout` | `SPDL_MYSQLSTORE_QUERY_TIMEOUT` | `10s` |

The selection flag is `--store-type mysql` (`SPDL_STORE_TYPE=mysql`). Explicit
flags override nonempty environment variables, then configuration files, then
defaults. For remote MySQL, use a hostname with a trusted server certificate and
add `?tls=true` to the DSN; custom CA configuration follows the
[driver TLS documentation](https://github.com/go-sql-driver/mysql/tree/v1.10.1#tls).

| Symptom | Check |
| --- | --- |
| Unknown `mysql` store or flag | Rebuild both binaries from source containing `pkg/store/mysql`. |
| Connection refused / access denied | Database readiness, DSN host/port, password and MySQL account host restrictions. |
| Unknown database | Create the database first; Speedle creates only tables. |
| Missing tables or DDL denied | Start PMS first, or pre-create the schema; read-only ADS must set `MySQLInitSchema` to `false`. |
| Policy change is not visible | Same database in both DSNs, ADS watch enabled, polling delay, and no overriding `SPDL_*` variables. |

MySQL does not support Discover request collection or policy generation. See
[Pluggable Storage](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/store/) for transaction, snapshot and recovery details.

## etcd Setup

Source: https://engine.speedle.io/docs/store/etcd/

This walkthrough uses an **external etcd v3.6.14** server with a persistent Docker volume. PMS writes policies and ADS watches the same key prefix. The single-node example listens on loopback and uses plain HTTP for local development. Production TLS and cluster configuration follow the walkthrough.

### 1. Build Speedle

Prepare Bash, Git, curl, Docker and Go 1.26.10 or Go 1.27.3. Start Docker, then build the native services:


```bash
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/teramoby/speedle-plus.git
cd speedle-plus
mkdir -p bin
go build -o ./bin/ ./cmd/spctl ./cmd/speedle-pms ./cmd/speedle-ads
```

Run subsequent commands from this checkout. Keep local ports 2379, 6733 and 6734 available, or update the commands and configuration together.

### 2. Start an external etcd server

The named volume holds etcd's data. Only the client port is published to the host; the peer port remains inside this single-node container.


```bash
docker run --name speedle-etcd --detach \
  --publish 127.0.0.1:2379:2379 \
  --volume speedle-etcd-data:/etcd-data \
  gcr.io/etcd-development/etcd:v3.6.14 \
  /usr/local/bin/etcd \
  --name speedle-local \
  --data-dir /etcd-data \
  --listen-client-urls http://0.0.0.0:2379 \
  --advertise-client-urls http://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --listen-peer-urls http://0.0.0.0:2380 \
  --initial-advertise-peer-urls http://127.0.0.1:2380 \
  --initial-cluster speedle-local=http://127.0.0.1:2380 \
  --initial-cluster-token speedle-local-demo \
  --initial-cluster-state new
```

Wait for the v3 API to become healthy:


```bash
until docker exec speedle-etcd /usr/local/bin/etcdctl \
  --endpoints=http://localhost:2379 endpoint health
do
  sleep 1
done
```

If you already run etcd, skip the container commands and use its client endpoint below. See the [official container guide](https://etcd.io/docs/v3.6/op-guide/container/) for Docker networking details.

### 3. Configure the shared store

Create one configuration file for this local PMS/ADS pair:


```bash
mkdir -p etcd-demo
cat > etcd-demo/config.json <<'JSON'
{
  "storeConfig": {
    "storeType": "etcd",
    "storeProps": {
      "EtcdEndpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:2379",
      "EtcdKeyPrefix": "/speedle_ps/",
      "IsEmbeddedEtcd": false
    }
  },
  "enableWatch": true
}
JSON
```

PMS and ADS must use the **same endpoint and key prefix**. Keep the trailing slash in `/speedle_ps/`; use a separate prefix for each independent policy store. `IsEmbeddedEtcd: false` connects to your external server. `enableWatch: true` enables ADS updates through etcd watch events; no polling interval is configured.

### 4. Start PMS

In terminal A, start PMS and leave it running:


```bash
./bin/speedle-pms --config-file etcd-demo/config.json --endpoint 127.0.0.1:6733 --insecure=true
```

Wait for its REST listener to start. Plain HTTP is bound to loopback for this demo; see [Security](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/security/) for Speedle's own TLS and API authorization.

### 5. Create a policy

In terminal B, from the same checkout, grant Alice permission to read `book`:


```bash
curl -fsS -X POST http://127.0.0.1:6733/policy-mgmt/v1/service \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"etcd-demo","type":"application","policies":[{"name":"alice-read","effect":"grant","principals":[["user:alice"]],"permissions":[{"resource":"book","actions":["read"]}]}]}'
```

PMS returns the service and generated policy ID. The policy is now in etcd; no SQL schema or manual key initialization is needed.

### 6. Start ADS and verify authorization

In terminal C, start ADS with the same file and leave it running:


```bash
./bin/speedle-ads --config-file etcd-demo/config.json --endpoint 127.0.0.1:6734 --insecure=true
```

Wait for startup, then run these checks in terminal B. Alice is allowed:


```bash
curl -fsS -X POST http://127.0.0.1:6734/authz-check/v1/is-allowed \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"subject":{"principals":[{"type":"user","name":"alice"}]},"serviceName":"etcd-demo","resource":"book","action":"read"}'
```

Expected: `{"allowed":true,"reason":0}`. Bob has no matching grant:


```bash
curl -fsS -X POST http://127.0.0.1:6734/authz-check/v1/is-allowed \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"subject":{"principals":[{"type":"user","name":"bob"}]},"serviceName":"etcd-demo","resource":"book","action":"read"}'
```

Expected: `{"allowed":false,"reason":3}`.

### 7. Verify stored keys and automatic updates

Inspect only the keys in this policy store:


```bash
docker exec speedle-etcd /usr/local/bin/etcdctl \
  --endpoints=http://localhost:2379 get /speedle_ps/ --prefix --keys-only
```

The output includes keys for `etcd-demo` under `/speedle_ps/services/`. Treat the keys as backend-managed data and make policy changes through PMS.

Add a deny while ADS remains running:


```bash
curl -fsS -X POST http://127.0.0.1:6733/policy-mgmt/v1/service/etcd-demo/policy \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"alice-deny","effect":"deny","principals":[["user:alice"]],"permissions":[{"resource":"book","actions":["read"]}]}'
```

Repeat Alice's request from step 6. After the asynchronous watch update, it should return `{"allowed":false,"reason":1}`. Repeat the request if synchronization is still in progress. ADS does not need a restart for this normal policy update.

### 8. Save a snapshot and verify persistence

Take a live snapshot, inspect it, and copy it outside the container:


```bash
docker exec speedle-etcd /usr/local/bin/etcdctl \
  --endpoints=http://localhost:2379 snapshot save /etcd-data/speedle-snapshot.db
docker exec speedle-etcd /usr/local/bin/etcdutl \
  snapshot status /etcd-data/speedle-snapshot.db --write-out=table
docker cp speedle-etcd:/etcd-data/speedle-snapshot.db ./etcd-demo/speedle-snapshot.db
```

A snapshot contains the **whole etcd cluster's keyspace**, including other prefixes. Store backups on separate protected storage. See [Disaster recovery](https://etcd.io/docs/v3.6/op-guide/recovery/) for restore and membership procedures.

Stop PMS and ADS with Ctrl+C before this restart check:


```bash
docker restart speedle-etcd
```

Run the health check in step 2, restart PMS and ADS with the same configuration, then repeat Alice's request. It should still return `{"allowed":false,"reason":1}`. The named volume retains data across the container restart.

For a disaster restore, stop policy writers, restore the snapshot into new data directories as described by etcd, and restart ADS so it reads the restored store before serving decisions. Recheck authorization after recovery; a previously running cache is not proof that it contains the restored policy set.

### Production: TLS, authentication and clusters

Deploy etcd with a trusted server certificate, a certificate SAN matching the endpoint hostname, and client-certificate validation. Then configure PMS/ADS to use HTTPS and their client credentials:

```json
{
  "storeConfig": {
    "storeType": "etcd",
    "storeProps": {
      "EtcdEndpoint": "https://etcd.example.com:2379",
      "EtcdKeyPrefix": "/speedle_ps/",
      "IsEmbeddedEtcd": false,
      "EtcdTLSTrustedCAFile": "/etc/speedle/etcd/ca.crt",
      "EtcdTLSCertFile": "/etc/speedle/etcd/client.crt",
      "EtcdTLSKeyFile": "/etc/speedle/etcd/client.key",
      "EtcdTLSServerName": "etcd.example.com",
      "EtcdTLSInsecureSkipVerify": false
    }
  },
  "enableWatch": true
}
```

These paths are on the PMS/ADS machine. Restrict private-key access to the service account. TLS to etcd is configured separately from TLS on Speedle's REST/gRPC listeners.

The adapter exposes certificate options and does not expose etcd username/password properties. For etcd RBAC, use client-certificate Common Names as user identities with `--client-cert-auth=true` and authentication enabled. Grant PMS read/write access to its prefix and ADS the permissions its enabled features require. See the official [TLS](https://etcd.io/docs/v3.6/op-guide/security/) and [RBAC](https://etcd.io/docs/v3.6/op-guide/authentication/rbac/) guides for server configuration and roles. A key prefix groups data; access control requires RBAC.

For high availability, follow the official [three-member cluster example](https://etcd.io/docs/v3.6/op-guide/container/#running-a-3-node-etcd-cluster) and protect client and peer traffic. The single-node demo cannot tolerate loss of its only member. The current `EtcdEndpoint` property accepts one endpoint string; provide a reachable client URL for your deployment.

### Configuration reference and troubleshooting

| Property | Flag | Environment variable | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `EtcdEndpoint` | `--etcdstore-endpoint` | `SPDL_ETCDSTORE_ENDPOINT` | `localhost:2379` |
| `EtcdKeyPrefix` | `--etcdstore-keyprefix` | `SPDL_ETCDSTORE_KEYPREFIX` | `/speedle_ps/` |
| `IsEmbeddedEtcd` | `--etcdstore-isembedded` | `SPDL_ETCDSTORE_ISEMBEDDED` | `false` |
| `EmbeddedEtcdDataDir` | `--etcdstore-embeddedDataDir` | `SPDL_ETCDSTORE_EMBEDDEDDATADIR` | Empty; embedded mode only |
| `EtcdTLSTrustedCAFile` | `--etcdstore-tls-ca` | `SPDL_ETCDSTORE_TLS_CA` | Empty |
| `EtcdTLSCertFile` | `--etcdstore-tls-cert` | `SPDL_ETCDSTORE_TLS_CERT` | Empty |
| `EtcdTLSKeyFile` | `--etcdstore-tls-key` | `SPDL_ETCDSTORE_TLS_KEY` | Empty |
| `EtcdTLSServerName` | `--etcdstore-tls-serverName` | `SPDL_ETCDSTORE_TLS_SERVERNAME` | Empty |
| `EtcdTLSInsecureSkipVerify` | `--etcdstore-tls-insecureSkipVerify` | `SPDL_ETCDSTORE_TLS_INSECURESKIPVERIFY` | `false` |

Explicit flags override nonempty environment variables, then configuration files, then defaults. Select the backend with `--store-type etcd` or `SPDL_STORE_TYPE=etcd`. Additional TLS options are `EtcdTLSAllowedCN` (`--etcdstore-tls-allowedCN`) and `EtcdTLSCRLFile` (`--etcdstore-tls-crlFile`).

Embedded mode (`IsEmbeddedEtcd: true`) is for local development/tests and uses the fixed local etcd port. This guide keeps etcd independent from PMS/ADS so its data directory and lifecycle are managed explicitly.

| Symptom | Check |
| --- | --- |
| Connection refused or startup stalls | etcd endpoint health, client port, host/container address and firewall. |
| PMS writes but ADS has no service | Same endpoint and key prefix, including the trailing slash. |
| Changes do not reach ADS | Watch enabled, connectivity and watch errors in ADS logs; restart ADS to reload after a recovery. |
| TLS hostname or CA error | HTTPS endpoint, certificate SAN, trusted CA path and server-name setting. |
| Permission denied | Client certificate identity, enabled RBAC roles and prefix permissions. |

Return to [Pluggable Storage](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/store/) for backend interfaces and configuration precedence.

Store failures follow the same policy as every built-in store: ADS defaults to deny with an error after detecting unavailability, stays running and retries, and resumes after a successful complete reload. See [store failures and cached authorization](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/store/#store-failures-and-cached-authorization) for the optional finite grace period and its revocation delay.

## MongoDB Setup

Source: https://engine.speedle.io/docs/store/mongodb/

This walkthrough uses **MongoDB 7.0.16** as a single-node replica set with a persistent Docker volume. PMS writes policies and ADS follows the same database through a change stream. The example listens on loopback without authentication for local development. Production authentication, TLS and replica set configuration follow the walkthrough.

MongoDB must run as a **replica set or sharded cluster**. ADS watches the database with a change stream, and replacing the whole policy store runs in a transaction; a standalone `mongod` supports neither. A single-node replica set is enough for development.

### 1. Build Speedle

Prepare Bash, Git, curl, Docker and Go 1.26.10 or Go 1.27.3. Start Docker, then build the native services:


```bash
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/teramoby/speedle-plus.git
cd speedle-plus
mkdir -p bin
go build -o ./bin/ ./cmd/spctl ./cmd/speedle-pms ./cmd/speedle-ads
```

Run subsequent commands from this checkout. Keep local ports 27017, 6733 and 6734 available, or update the commands and configuration together.

### 2. Start MongoDB

The named volume holds MongoDB's data. `--replSet` starts `mongod` as a member of the replica set `speedle-rs`; only the database port is published, on loopback.


```bash
docker run --name speedle-mongodb --detach \
  --publish 127.0.0.1:27017:27017 \
  --volume speedle-mongodb-data:/data/db \
  mongo:7.0.16 \
  --replSet speedle-rs --bind_ip_all
```

Wait for the server to accept commands:


```bash
until docker exec speedle-mongodb mongosh --quiet \
  --eval 'db.adminCommand({ping: 1}).ok' >/dev/null 2>&1
do
  sleep 1
done
```

If you already run a MongoDB replica set, skip the container commands and step 3, and use its connection string below. See the [official Docker image](https://hub.docker.com/_/mongo) for container details.

### 3. Initialize the replica set

Initialize the replica set once, with this server as its only member, and wait until it becomes primary:


```bash
docker exec speedle-mongodb mongosh --quiet --eval \
  'rs.initiate({_id: "speedle-rs", members: [{_id: 0, host: "127.0.0.1:27017"}]})'
until docker exec speedle-mongodb mongosh --quiet \
  --eval 'db.hello().isWritablePrimary' | grep -qx true
do
  sleep 1
done
```

The member address `127.0.0.1:27017` is what clients are told to connect to, so it must be reachable from PMS and ADS. It works here because the port is published on the same loopback address. The configuration is stored in the volume; do not run `rs.initiate` again after a restart.

### 4. Configure the shared store

Create one configuration file for this local PMS/ADS pair:


```bash
mkdir -p mongodb-demo
cat > mongodb-demo/config.json <<'JSON'
{
  "storeConfig": {
    "storeType": "mongodb",
    "storeProps": {
      "MongoURI": "mongodb://127.0.0.1:27017/?replicaSet=speedle-rs",
      "MongoDatabase": "speedle_demo"
    }
  },
  "enableWatch": true
}
JSON
```

PMS and ADS must use the **same deployment and database**. Use a separate database for each independent policy store; the store keeps services and functions in its `services` and `functions` collections. MongoDB creates the database and collections on the first write, so no schema initialization is needed. `enableWatch: true` enables ADS updates through the change stream; no polling interval is configured.

### 5. Start PMS

In terminal A, start PMS and leave it running:


```bash
./bin/speedle-pms --config-file mongodb-demo/config.json --endpoint 127.0.0.1:6733 --insecure=true
```

Wait for its REST listener to start. Plain HTTP is bound to loopback for this demo; see [Security](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/security/) for Speedle's own TLS and API authorization.

### 6. Create a policy

In terminal B, from the same checkout, grant Alice permission to read `book`:


```bash
curl -fsS -X POST http://127.0.0.1:6733/policy-mgmt/v1/service \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"mongodb-demo","type":"application","policies":[{"name":"alice-read","effect":"grant","principals":[["user:alice"]],"permissions":[{"resource":"book","actions":["read"]}]}]}'
```

PMS returns the service and generated policy ID. The policy is now in MongoDB.

### 7. Start ADS and verify authorization

In terminal C, start ADS with the same file and leave it running:


```bash
./bin/speedle-ads --config-file mongodb-demo/config.json --endpoint 127.0.0.1:6734 --insecure=true
```

Wait for startup, then run these checks in terminal B. Alice is allowed:


```bash
curl -fsS -X POST http://127.0.0.1:6734/authz-check/v1/is-allowed \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"subject":{"principals":[{"type":"user","name":"alice"}]},"serviceName":"mongodb-demo","resource":"book","action":"read"}'
```

Expected: `{"allowed":true,"reason":0}`. Bob has no matching grant:


```bash
curl -fsS -X POST http://127.0.0.1:6734/authz-check/v1/is-allowed \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"subject":{"principals":[{"type":"user","name":"bob"}]},"serviceName":"mongodb-demo","resource":"book","action":"read"}'
```

Expected: `{"allowed":false,"reason":3}`.

### 8. Verify stored documents and automatic updates

Inspect the service document; the service name is its `_id`:


```bash
docker exec speedle-mongodb mongosh speedle_demo --quiet --eval \
  'db.services.find({}, {"policies.name": 1, "policies.effect": 1}).toArray()'
```

The output includes `_id: 'mongodb-demo'` with the `alice-read` grant. Treat the documents as backend-managed data and make policy changes through PMS.

Add a deny while ADS remains running:


```bash
curl -fsS -X POST http://127.0.0.1:6733/policy-mgmt/v1/service/mongodb-demo/policy \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"alice-deny","effect":"deny","principals":[["user:alice"]],"permissions":[{"resource":"book","actions":["read"]}]}'
```

Repeat Alice's request from step 7. After the asynchronous change-stream update, it should return `{"allowed":false,"reason":1}`. Repeat the request if synchronization is still in progress. ADS does not need a restart for this normal policy update.

### 9. Save a backup and verify persistence

Dump the policy database to an archive and copy it outside the container:


```bash
docker exec speedle-mongodb mongodump --quiet \
  --db speedle_demo --archive=/tmp/speedle-demo.archive
docker cp speedle-mongodb:/tmp/speedle-demo.archive ./mongodb-demo/speedle-demo.archive
```

The archive contains only the `speedle_demo` database. Store backups on separate protected storage. To restore it, stop policy writers and run `mongorestore --drop --archive=...` against the primary; see [Back up and restore with MongoDB tools](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/backup-and-restore-tools/).

Stop PMS and ADS with Ctrl+C before this restart check:


```bash
docker restart speedle-mongodb
```

Run both wait loops in steps 2 and 3, skipping `rs.initiate`, restart PMS and ADS with the same configuration, then repeat Alice's request. It should still return `{"allowed":false,"reason":1}`. The named volume retains the data and the replica set configuration across the container restart.

After a restore, restart ADS so it reads the restored store before serving decisions. Recheck authorization after recovery; a previously running cache is not proof that it contains the restored policy set.

### Production: authentication, TLS and replica sets

Enable access control, give PMS and ADS separate users, and connect over TLS. PMS needs `readWrite` on the policy database. ADS only reads and watches, so the built-in `read` role is enough, and its user cannot change policies:

```javascript
use speedle
db.createUser({user: "speedle-pms", pwd: passwordPrompt(), roles: [{role: "readWrite", db: "speedle"}]})
db.createUser({user: "speedle-ads", pwd: passwordPrompt(), roles: [{role: "read", db: "speedle"}]})
```

Then give each service its own connection string:

```json
{
  "storeConfig": {
    "storeType": "mongodb",
    "storeProps": {
      "MongoURI": "mongodb://speedle-ads:replace-me@mongo1.example.com:27017,mongo2.example.com:27017,mongo3.example.com:27017/?replicaSet=speedle-rs&authSource=speedle&tls=true&tlsCAFile=/etc/speedle/mongodb/ca.pem",
      "MongoDatabase": "speedle"
    }
  },
  "enableWatch": true
}
```

The CA path is on the PMS/ADS machine. Credentials in a URI must be percent-encoded, and a configuration file containing them must be readable only by the service account; you can supply the URI through `SPDL_MONGOSTORE_URI` instead. Every option of the [MongoDB connection string](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/reference/connection-string/) is passed to the Go driver unchanged, including client certificates (`tlsCertificateKeyFile`) and other authentication mechanisms. TLS to MongoDB is configured separately from TLS on Speedle's REST/gRPC listeners.

Access control on a replica set also requires authentication between members, with a key file or X.509 certificates. See the official guides to [deploy a self-managed replica set with keyfile authentication](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/deploy-replica-set-with-keyfile-access-control/) and [configure TLS](https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/tutorial/configure-ssl/).

For high availability, use at least three data-bearing members and list several of them in the connection string. The single-node demo cannot tolerate loss of its only member. While a new primary is elected, writes through PMS can fail; retry them after the election.

### Configuration reference and troubleshooting

| Property | Flag | Environment variable | Default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `MongoURI` | `--mongostore_uri` | `SPDL_MONGOSTORE_URI` | `mongodb://localhost:27017` |
| `MongoDatabase` | `--mongostore_database` | `SPDL_MONGOSTORE_DATABASE` | `speedleplus` |

Explicit flags override nonempty environment variables, then configuration files, then defaults. Select the backend with `--store-type mongodb` or `SPDL_STORE_TYPE=mongodb`. For embedded use, import `pkg/store/mongodb` and pass these properties to `store.NewStore`.

Behaviour to know when operating the store:

- Replacing the whole store (`WritePolicyStore`) runs in one transaction. It keeps supplied policy IDs and generates missing ones. On a standalone server it fails without changing existing data.
- Deleting all services or functions keeps the collections, so the change stream stays open and ADS removes the cached entries.
- Reading the whole store reads services and functions in one snapshot on a replica set or sharded cluster.
- If the change stream ends, ADS reopens it with a backoff of up to 30 seconds, then reloads the whole store, so changes made in between are not lost. Until then it keeps serving its last loaded policies.
- Discover request collection and policy generation are not supported; they are available with the file and etcd stores.

| Symptom | Check |
| --- | --- |
| Server selection timeout at startup | Replica set initialized and primary, the member host in `rs.conf()` reachable from PMS/ADS, URI host and port, firewall. |
| ADS exits with `The $changeStream stage is only supported on replica sets` | The deployment is a standalone `mongod`; use a replica set or sharded cluster. |
| PMS writes but ADS has no service | Same URI deployment and `MongoDatabase` name in both configurations. |
| Changes do not reach ADS | Watch enabled; change stream and reopen errors in ADS logs, which repeat until ADS reaches the database again. |
| Authentication failed | User, password encoding, `authSource` and the role on the policy database. |
| TLS error | `tls=true`, CA file path and certificate host names. |

Return to [Pluggable Storage](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/store/) for backend interfaces and configuration precedence.

Store failures follow the same policy as every built-in store: ADS defaults to deny with an error after detecting unavailability, stays running and retries, and resumes after a successful complete reload. See [store failures and cached authorization](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/store/#store-failures-and-cached-authorization) for the optional finite grace period and its revocation delay.

## Security

Source: https://engine.speedle.io/docs/security/

### Protect both API transports

Speedle's standalone PMS and ADS expose **REST and gRPC**. Both now use the same `--insecure`, `--cert`, `--key`, `--client-cert` and `--force-client-cert` transport settings. Invalid certificates or trust configuration cause startup to fail; secure mode does not fall back to plaintext.

TLS encrypts the connection and authenticates the server. To require authenticated clients, provide a client CA with `--client-cert` **and** set `--force-client-cert=true`. Without that flag, a configured CA validates a client certificate only when the client supplies one. TLS alone does not authorize an administrator or provide bearer-token validation. Use an authenticated gateway or equivalent access controls for management, diagnosis and discovery endpoints. The `--enable-authz` flag does not provide a built-in endpoint authorization policy.

### Listen addresses and compatibility

| Service | Default REST address | Default gRPC address |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PMS | `0.0.0.0:6733` | disabled until `--grpc-endpoint` is set |
| ADS | `0.0.0.0:6734` | disabled until `--grpc-endpoint` is set |

REST and gRPC listen addresses are configured separately. Setting `--endpoint` alone does not enable gRPC. Explicitly use `--grpc-endpoint 127.0.0.1:50001` for PMS or `127.0.0.1:50002` for ADS. `127.0.0.1:0` requests an ephemeral port for isolated tests; specify an IPv6 address explicitly when needed.

Configuration precedence is command line, then `SPDL_*` environment variables, then JSON, then defaults. The gRPC overrides are `--grpc-endpoint`, `SPDL_GRPC_ENDPOINT`, and `serverConfig.grpcEndpoint`. See the [current proto contracts](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/api/) for RPC namespaces and client generation.

### Generate certificates for a local test

Build the binaries using the [quick start](https://engine.speedle.io/quick-start/). From the repository root, use Go 1.26.10 or Go 1.27.3 (or a newer patch on the same release branch) to generate a local CA plus separate server/client certificates. The server certificate has SANs for `localhost`, `127.0.0.1` and `::1`; private keys use mode 0600. These **24-hour demonstration certificates** are not production credentials. The generator refuses to overwrite existing files: choose a new output directory when regenerating.


```bash
go run ./website/tests/examples/certificates --out ./tls
```


### Start mutually authenticated services

Initialize a fresh policy file once, with both services stopped:


```bash
printf '{}\n' > docs-policies.json
```


Start PMS in one terminal:


```bash
./bin/speedle-pms --store-type file --filestore-loc ./docs-policies.json \
  --endpoint 127.0.0.1:6733 --grpc-endpoint 127.0.0.1:50001 \
  --cert ./tls/server.crt --key ./tls/server.key \
  --client-cert ./tls/ca.crt --force-client-cert=true
```


Start ADS in a second terminal:


```bash
./bin/speedle-ads --store-type file --filestore-loc ./docs-policies.json \
  --endpoint 127.0.0.1:6734 --grpc-endpoint 127.0.0.1:50002 \
  --cert ./tls/server.crt --key ./tls/server.key \
  --client-cert ./tls/ca.crt --force-client-cert=true
```


Run both terminals from the same repository root. Keep them open; stop each with Ctrl-C when finished. Production certificates must cover the actual DNS names/IPs and come from your organization's trusted CA.

### Connect with spctl and curl


```bash
./bin/spctl --pms-endpoint https://127.0.0.1:6733/policy-mgmt/v1/ \
  --skipverify=false --cacert ./tls/ca.crt --cert ./tls/client.crt --key ./tls/client.key \
  get service --all
```



```bash
curl --fail --silent --show-error --cacert ./tls/ca.crt \
  --cert ./tls/client.crt --key ./tls/client.key \
  https://127.0.0.1:6733/policy-mgmt/v1/service
```


An empty store returns `[]`. Omitting the client certificate fails the TLS handshake. `spctl` uses `--cacert` for server trust and `--cert`/`--key` for its own identity; `--client-cert` and `--force-client-cert` are server flags. Keep `--skipverify=false` (the default).

For gRPC, configure the generated client's channel with the same CA, a matching server name, and the client certificate/key. PMS uses `pb.PolicyManager`; ADS uses `pb.Evaluator`. An insecure channel must fail against these TLS endpoints.

### Local plaintext development

Only an explicit `--insecure=true` enables plaintext for both transports. Bind REST and gRPC to loopback for that mode. Do not publish these unauthenticated endpoints or trust principal names/attributes supplied by untrusted callers. The [token asserter](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/assertor/) validates a configured identity token; it does not authenticate every PMS/ADS caller or replace endpoint access controls.

## Usecases

Source: https://engine.speedle.io/docs/usecases/

### Application specific policies

Alex Chan is a developer who is implementing a simple application with golang. His application requires Authorization and he doesn’t want to re-invent the wheel. Alex can use an open source choice like Speedle for Authorization.

### Centalized policy enforcement and management

Jin Chen is a security manager of multinational company. His team monitor dozens of internal systems. Different systems use different authorization mechanisms, different policy languages. They are eager to find a solution to manage all these systems efficiently.

- Centralized policy management
- Flexible policy model which fits for all the systems
- Easy to integrate with different systems, from OS to middleware to applications
- Scalable to support all the systems
- Efficient

### Single plane of glass for authorization across the fleet

TTH Inc. is a startup cloud company. They offer a cloud native environment to their customers. The environment consists of Linux, Docker, Kubernetes, and Istio. Security is top priority for TTH offerings. They define a comprehensive authorization model, create policies in Linux, Docker, Kubernetes, Istio in different terminals and using different policy languages. Can we make their lives easier?

- Centralized policy management
- Unified authorization policy model for Linux, Docker, Kubernetes, Istio
- Scalable for cloud operation
- Efficient
- Easy to integrate with Linux, Docker, Kubernetes, Istio
- Open Source

## Logging Framework

Source: https://engine.speedle.io/docs/logging/

### Overview

The following two open source projects are used to process log messages,

```
1. https://github.com/sirupsen/logrus
2. https://github.com/natefinch/lumberjack
```

Logrus is a structured logger for Go (golang), and completely API compatible with the golang standard library logger. Note that logrus doesn't support log rotation, and it is exactly the reason why we introduce the second project lumberjack, which provides a rolling logger. Logrus communicates with lumberjack using the io.Writer interface, please refer to the following diagram,

<img src="https://engine.speedle.io/img/speedle/logger.jpg" alt="Speedle Logging" width="370" height="230" loading="lazy">

### Logging Configuration

There are two ways to configure logging for Speedle, either via command line arguments or via configuration file.

#### Configure logging via command line arguments

All the available command line arguments are listed below. The level, formatter and reportcaller settings configure logrus; file/rotation settings configure lumberjack.

```
--log-level string
--log-formatter string
--log-reportcaller bool
--log-filename string
--log-maxsize int
--log-maxbackups int
--log-maxage int
--log-localtime bool
--log-compress bool
```

The detailed info of each item is in the following table. Note that any of the following configuration item is optional. If none of them is configured, then the log messages with info level or above will be written to the stderr in text format by default.

| Configuration Item | Description                                                                                                                           | Default Value                                                                                  |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| --log-level        | log level, available levels are panic, fatal, error, warn, info and debug                                                             | info                                                                                           |
| --log-formatter    | log formatter, available values are text and json                                                                                     | text                                                                                           |
| --log-reportcaller | control whether get the caller info (file, line and function) included in the log entries                                             | false                                                                                          |
| --log-filename     | log file name                                                                                                                         | no default value. If it isn't configured, then log messages are written to stderr              |
| --log-maxsize      | maximum size in megabytes of the log file before it gets rotated. It's only valid when "--log-filename" is configured                 | 100                                                                                            |
| --log-maxbackups   | maximum number of old log files to retain. It's only valid when "--log-filename" is configured                                        | 0, which means to retain all old log files (though MaxAge may still cause them to get deleted) |
| --log-maxage       | maximum number of days to retain old log files. It's only valid when "--log-filename" is configured                                   | 0, which means not to remove old log files based on age                                        |
| --log-localtime    | control whether local time is used for formatting the timestamps in backup files. It's only valid when "--log-filename" is configured | false, which means to use UTC time                                                             |
| --log-compress     | control whether the rotated log files should be compressed. It's only valid when "--log-filename" is configured                       | false, which means not to perform compression                                                  |

The following two examples are in text and json format respectively,

```
# text
time="2015-03-26T01:27:38-04:00" level=debug msg="Started observing beach" animal=walrus number=8
```

```
# json
{"animal":"walrus","level":"info","msg":"A group of walrus emerges from the
ocean","size":10,"time":"2014-03-10 19:57:38.562264131 -0400 EDT"}
```

#### Configure logging via configuration file

An example is as below. Again, any configuration item is optional as well.

```json
{
    "logConfig": {
        "level": "info",
        "formatter": "text",
        "setReportCaller": false,
        "rotationConfig": {
            "filename": "/mnt/logs/speedle.log",
            "maxSize": 20,
            "maxBackups": 5,
            "maxAge": 0,
            "LocalTime": false,
            "compress": false
        }
    }
}
```

### Best practices for configuring logging

If Speedle runs as docker containers, then it's more natural to to use the docker's json-file logging driver instead of the open source project natefinch/lumberjack to rotate log files, accordingly json-file logging driver is recommended for this case. Only sirupsen/logrus is needed, in other words, users don't need to configure anything for natefinch/lumberjack at all in this case.

All docker related configuration items, including logging, are configured in /etc/docker/daemon.json. Please refer to [docker json-file](https://docs.docker.com/config/containers/logging/json-file/) to get more detailed info on how to configure json-file logging driver. The following snippet is an example,

```
{
  "log-driver": "json-file",
  "log-opts": {
    "max-size": "20m",
    "max-file": "10"
  }
}
```

In most cases, users don't need to configure sirupsen/logrus either. The default log level is info, and the default log format is text. So generally users only need to configure the logging if they want to change the log level or log format, otherwise they need to configure nothing since the default configuration is good enough.

### How to add new log messages

Firstly import the log package as below,

```go
import (
  log "github.com/sirupsen/logrus"
)
```

Secondly output any log messages anywhere you want. For example,

```go
  log.Debug("This is a debug log entry")
  log.Info("This is a info log entry")
  log.Warn("This is a warning log entry")
  log.Warning("This is a warning log entry again")
  log.Error("This is a error log entry")
```

Please refer to [speedle/logging/demo/demo.go](https://github.com/teramoby/speedle-plus/blob/master/pkg/logging/demo/demo.go) to get more detailed info.

### Integration with 3rd-party log collectors

Speedle logs can be easily integrated with 3rd-party log collectors, such as fluentd or filebeat. What the users need to do is to configure fluentd or filebeat to monitor the log files generated by Speedle. The following configuration snippet is an example of using fluentd's in_tail input plugin to collect docker containers' log, including Speedle's log of course if Speedle runs as containers.

```
    <source>
      @type tail
      path /var/lib/docker/containers/*/*.log
      pos_file /data/fluentd/fluentd.log.pos
      tag speedle.log
      <parse>
        @type json
        time_key time
        keep_time_key true
      </parse>
      refresh_interval 5
    </source>
```

Please refer to [fluentd](https://www.fluentd.org/) and [filebeat](https://www.elastic.co/products/beats/filebeat) official websites to get more detailed info.

## Versions

Source: https://engine.speedle.io/docs/versions/

### Speedle releases

Use the [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/teramoby/speedle-plus/releases) page for published versions and release notes. [v1.6.0](https://github.com/teramoby/speedle-plus/releases/tag/v1.6.0) is the version pinned by the current embedded Go walkthrough. Use an explicit released version for reproducible module dependencies; the [embedded guide](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/deployment-embeded/) explains the setup.

### Historical Oracle Speedle release

Version 0.1.0 was the original open-source release, including policy management, authorization decisions, the command-line tool and integration samples. The historical 0.2.0 planning note is not the current Speedle release roadmap.

## Integrations

Source: https://engine.speedle.io/integrations/

Speedle makes authorization decisions. A policy enforcement point (PEP) in your application, gateway or platform calls Speedle for each decision and enforces the result. The interfaces below are supported today.

### REST and gRPC APIs

Manage services, policies and roles through the Policy Management Service (PMS), and request runtime decisions from the Authorization Decision Service (ADS). Both expose REST APIs; start either server with `--grpc-endpoint` to enable its gRPC API.

- [Policy management API](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/api/management_api/)
- [Authorization decision API](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/api/decision_api/)
- [Token assertion webhook](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/api/asserter_api/)
- [API overview, including the PMS and ADS protos](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/api/)

### Embedded Go

Run the evaluator inside a Go application, without a separate PMS or ADS process. The [embedded mode guide](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/deployment-embeded/) builds a complete example with Go modules.

### SDKs

Client SDKs are available for Java, Go, Python, Node.js/TypeScript, Rust and C#/.NET. See [SDKs](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/sdks/).

### Policy stores

Use the built-in file, etcd, MySQL or MongoDB store, or implement the store interfaces for another backend. See [Pluggable storage](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/store/).

### Previous guides

The previous Istio, Kubernetes and Docker sample guides are no longer published. Use the interfaces above for new integrations.
